August 1st, 2:31 p.m.

It was in August that I began to cough.

It began very slowly, a dry, inner chest scabbish feeling which I ignored quite easily. It was not the kind of cough which leaves one shaking and embarrassed at a dinner party, rushing to the bathroom to wipe of his hands. No, it was not that sort of cough at all. This was simply a dry cough – neither the product of a cold or winter ills, certainly neither due to emotional stress (I’ve always had a remarkable physique, as pertains to colds and fevers, and had, through the most turbulent of times (I believe this was the product of my fraudulent childhood – that childhood which was called such but in no way resembled it, full of far too many concerns of which my dear playground compatriots understood nothing – my mother dissolving into depression and drink, an infirm and alzheimatic and partially violent but mostly miserable grandmother living with us, her income supporting but her emotional burden dragging each of us – I mean each – down into those depths which I cannot, cannot bear to remember – a toddling sister for whom I was forced to care (I was young yes, but who else would care for here? There were things she needed in this life - there are certain necessities which necessitate necessitating, I mean they must be met, and such excuses as childhood are not enough to fight back their need – now, this is a different sort of justice, and not the sort that you find many crying for, but the justice that dictates that each takes care of what must be taken care of – not the maxim “You mow your front lawn, and I will mow mine, and then everyone’s lawn will be mown”, but the darkling deep and hunger which absolutely imperiates that the lawns must be mown, and if neighbor Joe won’t mow his lawn it still must be mown – this was the justice I knew, and under it I grew strong and healthy, because I could not afford to be otherwise) and who would always remain a toddler, in some sense, as her body outgrew her and her mind remained locked in the tower of the terrible diagnosis of mental disacuity (another stone on a tumbling heap – the heap in its fall, while it falls – this has always been my interest – not the towering geometric spires, not long straight and regular or Stonehenge, but the falling, scattered – beauty here irrepressible, something more organic and natural than any frozen natural system (and by this I mean any natural system which is decontextualized to the point where it may be examined – not the Nature of scientists, no) but that living complex of system which is its absolute lack and may only be seen by completely dismembering one’s self from temporal perception and simply sensing – feeling – all things at once wind rain fire ice birds falling nest eggs cracking everything moving dying living being born time slipping up and around close and fertile and sucking up around the neck and pressing, pressing – smothering – that pattern most closely resembling a fractal, but so escaping it (and the fractal itself I take to be the living emblem of the artistic endeavor -) as to remain an empty symbol, a hollow remembrance like a history written by the dead) which resolved her to forever remaining foreign, stranger, isolate) because those whose rightful responsibility it was to care for her were sprawled hapless over the bathroom sink or the toilet or staring into the mirror terrified and revolted and unrecognizing of the lifeless eyes they saw and hating, hating – sinking deep into the OtherImage presented to them there and willing to forget because (and I do not blame them this) it was better to forget, an absent father whose presence ceaselessly made its absence felt) remained physically acute and calm and quite preserved as my nerves were made of steel or perhaps synthetic metals) nor physical calamity (I had had one cold in my life) nor smoking, as I had given up smoking quite long ago in favor of not smoking.

I would simply cough. Of course it raised some question in my silences, some gleaming interrogative to one so accustomed to good health. But I was busy. I needed to get things together for the gang – there was rent money to secure, chemicals to acquire (which they needed desperately – now, I am not so cold-hearted as to sit and listen still and somber while my dear friend An-D grimaced and whined and eventually screamed (at night, most precisely – it was always worse at night – sitting in a warm bathtub helped for a time, 20 minutes, maybe, but the relief was inconsequential) or Dorris hid in the corner, seeing delirious lady bug dots of red and untold paranoia in her tremens – to these needs I aspired, to fulfill the health and spiritual well-being of my flat-mates. I took care of everything. Now, I personally had no such head for chemicals, nor could I imagine the discomfort or restlessness of being wired so – it was my reasonable service to see to their needs, to organize, to lead – to come home to the earthy embrace of their thankfulness and gratitude.

So. Matters being arranged thus, I thought nothing of it until mid-December. I sat alone in my study (My study which is the windy rooftop with no garden and several holes staring out over the tops of the scattered villages and precincts of the Holy City, gazing to the pinnacle of the mount, a radio station TV spire, or down and up at the stretched out horizonal infinite of the river, watching the little citizens criss-crossing their great drawbridge – meditating Eliot’s denizens (although I knew he had it wrong – November is the cruelest month, but I said no such thing to him) – meditating the steel rain, the hydrated inferno of sulfurous plumages, monstrous birds of industry towering above the bridge – that holy mountain stretching across the continent, the country (But dry sterile thunder without rain / There is not even solitude in the mountains / But red sullen faces sneer and snarl / From doors of mudcracked houses) – meditating everything beneath me, the warmly turning uxorial gears of happy household in the tenement womb beneath me – the whole city my nest, these materials beneath my fingers lustrous eggs I thought upon to hatch, I warmed with my sullen sunsets and red, snapping dragons filtering across the grayish and urbane clouds from the sun – then – I held the tissue to my face and coughed and held out red droplets and heart murmur for my own examination, all arranged in the ubiquitous ease of incalculable forces plotting above me – that sad strain on easy-mind of knowing circumstances tie together far beyond my whimsies of chance or happenstance –

some unknowable and terrible pattern in the blood - it laced between my fingers, over the ovary lines and stretching penumbras of the palm - my sight was fixated on it - trying to focus on each particle at once and seeing nothing - some deep and terrible portent which at one time would have been seen in entrails of goats above an altar and in dark whisperlings and - my mind slipped quickly away from all taken in by the eyes - light became illusory static - the black/white binary snowstorm of the tv screen at late night and I drunk and very drunk and sunk well into my self.

I felt foetid and diseased. not the quick, puncturing debilitation of the daily or temporal sickness - but something of a cancer. some deep corruption in the enlightened quarks of my smallest superstructures - some red tint to the pure white vision - I closed my eyes and let the wind whisper over me, hand held in front of my darkened sockets. I knew that some taint had slipped into the evening, had soaked into the smog-shaped clouds, had penetrated the cadmium smokestacks of the City.

I couldn't name the shapes I saw in the distance. Strange, monstrous shadows reflecting in the skyline above an unbelieving city. I saw them there and knew that the entirety of the city slept or fucked or drank themselves to death unaware of the not-clouds and not-stars which hung above them watching, hungry. I had recently purchased a box of crayons from the drugstore, the largest selection of colors available, which, at this time, had sprawled and ballooned from the 16 of my childhood into a zoneless flesh of 248 colors, all of them patinous and wretched mutations of familiar red and black and blue - I spread them all beneath me on the quartz-spattered rooftop, and knelt there, feeling the texture of the paper and the wax and drinking it in with my skin - reassured by the simplicity of touch - hungry for it - looking for a color that could describe the sky I saw with noone, alone in my head on the rooftops.  
  
celadon  
cadmium  
heliotrope  
gamboge

It seemed to me, considering the reddened specks on my palm, that I had coughed up some drops of an alternate existence - aborted fetuses of another me that were smeared on my hand and my sleeve. I straightaway made up my mind to share this bit of news with my long time friend and eternal compatriot confidant, Dorris. I wiped my sleeve on the back of my mouth and got up from my desk, which is an old cracked flower pot where nothing grows, and swung down to the elevator, which is the corner of the roof, turning around and grabbing its edges to lower myself into the apartment window. I arrived at an entirely opportune moment.

Now, Dorris is a helluva girl who drinks half a gallon of vodka per day. Dorris is quite short and packs a helluva punch which she is not afraid to use; often Dorris has come across trouble due to bar fights or socking grown men in the jaw or the groin or breaking beer bottles over their fat pasty skulls. I cannot tell you how many times I have had to patiently explain to officers of the law that, "Look, this is my Dorris and she's quite fine and well, and I consistently suggest that you leave her be as she's mental disorders which interfere with her hearing your fat piggish gibber." Now, whether due to her glare or my diplomatic negotiations (or, more likely, a simple disbelief in four foot Dorris being the cause of so much tribulation), she rarely spent time in jail and has never been brought up officially, neither in federal nor civil courts, on charges of assault. Dorris does not work but rather stays up late drinking and swearing and carving little and genuine handmade figurines of Scottish generals and kings, which she believes to be her calling and life's work as an Artist.

August 45th, 9:86 p.m.

After much pontification with Dorris, I realized that the coughs were vibrations into the fabric of my existence, strange shimmerings of an alternate and static dream which rumbled beneath the surface of every nightlight. With urgency I sat to write Rebekah, knowing that, somehow, Rebekah could dissipate the strange shapes I felt in my stomach. I coughed and spattered little droplets of blood onto the page that look like this:

Dearest Rebekah,

I am experiencing a thing which I have no words for. It is as if I see a horrid shadow beneath all my daily events, and the self I see in the mirror is some debaucherous actor. When I look in the mirror, I sometimes see myself as if the walls of my eyes had expanded and become the sky itself, which I see and am perched beneath and redistributed among sparrows and I, at a sharp crack of unknown noise, startle and light and dart, thousands of eyes in thousands of directions, each sky finding its own other branch and thousands sets of seeing-each-others multiplied and startled and lighting, each disunified I into the smallest bright-white and deep center-sun hydrogen-heat pixel, burning deep and deep and sinking into ash-gray flesh of cheeks beneath red-warm flare of apocalyptic sunshine, the last dim sun of licking itself to sleep and sinking into deep and deep forever sleep of sinking, contracting, deriving deep or out into the longest compressed horizonal infinite and expanding, straight line slight and massless and piercing its own met ends - branches holding the world in its roots - and sinking deep or deep into the darkest sleep, and only bright white stars and teeth, or bird-like points of nothingness in nothing.

Hope this has helped you access the symbolic whatnots of my experiential inner landscape.

Yours,

Ich.

Sepember , 34:1 p.p.

I felt as if I had two lives which were incommensurable, one with another. I had one life which I saw in sound waves which felt like pure white fire incinerative in my deepest deep and burnt everything, pure and crisp leaving no ashes only a pale, throbbing pain and a joy which were linked with one another. This was the life which struck me unexpectedly, in the pale times in the morning when everyone slept, at dawn, before dawn after sleepless nights when sitting on the roof and staring at the city and suddenly struck by something so deep and unpredictable that I am nearly lost, if with others so suddenly drawn away from them and inward to the tabernacle of white fire that I would stutter out meaningless and automatic replies to their questions and not know what I had said - some thing that felt like death and sex all at once and at the same time so intense and precious and absolutely black, leaving me with shallow breath and a sortof ache in my stomach and the tops of my legs that I could only smile a real sick-like and sortof perverse smile and just keep sinking - lower, lower - this death thing, this erotic thing, this thing I felt in my chest was more than me, more powerful than anything I was or had felt and something into which I was subsumed - whole cities melting and tipping and sinking into the volcanic and fissure-black fault line - whole cities rocking on their axis and sinking into that mouth and going down and rolling around on the earth's tongue as they plunged, meeting no bottom, the fissure opening on the other side of the earth to continue spitting downward in a space which had no motion, only silence, death, lust.

That was one life.

And another life, a life of the morning. Not dawn, but the morning. Not coming, not going - but a perpetually clear and soft-white glow of singing things and the morning. A life of sure surfaces and non-reflective ice, pale black and made of yellow, comforting and calm and composed of firm surface structures.

Yellow and black.

I drove the car and wanted it to last forever. Mr. Bright-Side by the Killers and a B-side from Jet poured out from my radio while the heart bled its total separation. I wondered if I would remember this or write it down, or if I would forget and be so bereft by lack of memory that I would make one up and write that down, and felt deep down my separateness and oneness with the irrecoverability of everything. I thought about books and writing and the great American dream of the Writer which was stabbing me in the chest. I wrote this all down in snatches and fragments and half-hidden whispers because I rarely finished books and so only know how to give glimpses and flashes and great brilliant burnouts and aftereffects, and nothing much of endings. I had stopped driving to scribble and was becoming quite late in the parking lot, but I didn't want the world to know I existed, could hardly make appointments with all this blood in my mouth and this red, sick song in my veins I can't shake. I just kept listening, wanting to sing with my mouth absolutely stoppered by another song and one more and another, and asked someThing or Anything to redeem this and these minutes.

There was a man outside the bus station waiting for a taxi. He was waiting for a subway car and a train. He was in his parking lot in a car and scribbling something down or nothing. He was scribbling grocery lists. He was scribbling suicide notes. He was scribbling manic somethings in the rain. It was not raining. There was a film of static on the screen. I adjusted the antenna. He adjusted the antenna.

I saw a man on an island. I was swimming in the water there or disembodied. I was not there. He was not an island. There was no island.

I saw a man in an orange tree. He was eating apples. He was an old mythic beast of American dream I had seen there and my children had seen there and my children's children had seen there and Adam and Eve had seen there, great mysterious Myth who had been up there eating apples since the beginning of Time or farther back; way far back he's been there, I saw him eating apples scribbling apples scribbling stories, songs, and limericks.

I am never more alive than when he writes.

The time was a certain time. It was a certain day, a certain month. Certainly certain hours passed unnoticed, ripped from the shreds of the day and leaving the hanging cloth banging against the glassless window; I knew her then. I wrote her countless letters then and sent them on the wind. I sent them out the window – it was the only certain sand in the sinking hourglass. Hours passed unnoticed, certain minutes were unmissed. The suffering in edges of eyes which comes from misplacing time, or the passing by unnoticed of minutes in an abandoned, decaying crack of house with no glass to keep out rain, and no more attention paid to the encroaching grasses and dandelions than to the slowly widening edge of minutes well beyond my fingers. I marked the time. In letters; in the widening circle’s edge. The suffering in edges of eyes stared out from uncertain and glassless, empty, empty maws, but for my face. I knew her then. I wrote her countless letters. I sent them on the wind.

“Who has never killed an hour? Not casually or without thought, but carefully: a premeditated murder of minutes. The violence comes from a combination of giving up, not caring, and a resignation that getting past is all you can hope to accomplish. So you kill the hour. You do not work, you do not read, you do not daydream. If you sleep it is not because you need to sleep. And when at last it is over, there is no evidence, no weapon, no blood, and no body. The only clue might be the shadows beneath your eyes or a terribly thin line near the corner of your mouth indicating something has been suffered, that in the privacy of your life you have lost something and the loss is too empty to share.”

I was standing at the edge of a forest while I was doing this. every once in awhile, I would complete part of the stick and toss a piece into the forest. each time I did so, the noise emitting from the forest would change. it was distant, background noise, but ominous. some words presided over my bedtime, some ghostly shells of meaning hovered above my bed and sucked my blood – it was all for you, Rebekah – I see me, sleeping, peaceless, presided over by the moon – a pale-eyed diviner of intentions, a glassless judge of the hidden heart (O deceitful, deceitfully wicked) – I am bare beneath these images:

**if your pale body drifts through the rafters and your**

**tattered wrists drip / on the seams of my bedclothes,**

**until bed is red and clothes are red and**

**\` *I* am red – Rebekah, then,**

**what will I do?**

**Rebekah,**

**I hear you**

**thumping**

**on the window,**

**the poorest**

**imitation**

**of cattails.**

rock and roll has taken the place of the mother.

methadone and roses.

sometimes I wish I could still speak, and then I remember that there was a reason I stopped.

"basement- b-ball- when i-i'll go g-get the bottles- if- g-g'night."

as soon as my attention falls on myself I decimate every shred of sentence structure and speck of honesty left in the whole of Neverland.

every time you turn the garbage disposal on I try to tell you

an odd elation, all tied up in headaches and white fire and memories and blood.

stares at me, from underneath the water, sad and vacant, full of cracks and puddles, accusing me from where I left it.

ten minute silence between that paragraph and this. I break my paragraphs apart into short little bits, sometimes related

by subject, sometimes strung together and broken at random.

we stayed up all night reading children's stories to eachother. everybody cracks a little bit when they read. they were the only thing alive. and the birds, this morning. between times.

the last clank of the tracks before the coaster drops and the whole stomach lurches free from the body

to chew it up. to find the holes and the dark spots and punch through them like a punctuation mark.

there is always laughter, to cover, and poems, to redeem

creative frenzy, for me, is much like orgasm

ticking clocks and thin electrical buzzing.

the degree of brokenness you're coming out of; the silences you're breaking.

...for the last time, it was fall, it was orange out, I was in the driveway. I was coming home, I don't know from where, I hadn't slept in several days. I thought I was dying. my memory is really fuzzy around this point, but I think I started crying in the driveway. I don't know. my sister was out there, sitting at her picnic table, digging in the dirt,

I really only have an impression and the bare bones of the experience and the emotion

smoking stinks. eat yer yams. don't lie to the television. grow up to be a doctor or else. the garbage man is watching.

so i'm writing this book about starfish, right? and I thought to myself, nobody's ever written a book about starfish before, it's sure to be a hit.

each ascending transformation is harder

I killed my dog and ate him.

I bought uranium for three dollars a pound.

I reinvented the bicycle.

this page is running out, and trees are dying everywhere

sometime between lives, 0:00

A gleaming red 'Open Always' flickers above and taunts them from the heavens. They watch as the airlock hisses open, the mouth of the whirlpool that regularly and, comforting in the mechanicity of its ticking, without a beat missed sucks everything into itself to destroy it, to pull the living things of the dark and torrid waters down through its metal filigree. Its mouth cracks open, inviting. The gang stumbles in but Ichabod hangs back. He checks the facade of late-night Meijer and examines it in a lens against their backs.

Battlements of small spears defend the balustrades from hordes of paean, orange-eyed pigeons that beetle-like peck around the tomato-red garbage cans that stand like sentinels at the entranceways. Three doors open and shut upon themselves. Inscribed on them, lining the frames in various degrees of font size, the large text overlaid with smaller text that shrinks into oblivion, rows of text that grow from a miniscule scrawl to giant whorls that encompass the frame and trail off into the blackness of the parking lot, large letters composed by rows upon rows of smaller letters, all an endlessly repeating series; strange, incomprehensible augurs:

“PER ME SI VA NELLA CITTA DOLENTE, / PER ME SI VA NELL’ ETTERNO DOLORE, / PER ME SI VA TRA LA PERDUTA GENTE.

“GIUSTIZIA MOSSE IL MIO ALTO FATTORE: / FECEMI LA DIVINA POTESTATE, / LA SOMMA SAPIENZA E ‘L PRIMO AMORE.

"This is a place of justice," whispers Ichabod to Dorris. But she floats ahead of him insensate and blissful and vulgar in her innocence.

they were butchering cattle behind the deli. a milk-white and semi-transparent screen of plastic sheeting ran its length; behind it, the ghostly figures of automaton butchers in blood-spattered surgeon's jackets could be dimly seen, maniacal at their labor, slicing strips of fat from the thighs and hanging them high on the blood-draining hooks of the steel ceiling fans. they bent over their labor behind safety goggles with a single-minded intensity of pursuit. on the other side of this divider (a one-sided mirror, for all effects - the poltergeists behind it could not see outside their labor to look at the solemn Doris tacking along beside a forlorn Ichabod in the oblong winds of midnight) the deli was dark and deserted, a haunted palace preserved in the panicked remnants of a feast, aborted by Ascension, by mass-Raptural Exodus and frozen in its ostentatious proceedings of glass plated meats and cheeses, of ceran-wrapped noodle-salads. a severed sow's head brooded darkly atop the meat-scale and grimaced at them attentively, eyeless. expectantly it smiled, frozen in its mirth for eternity. The head remained there, dim-eyed, grinning faintly, blood blackening between the teeth.

They walked between the nearness in the aisle ways beneath it vision, underneath its eyes their hands grasped at each other, their fat pink pinkies wrapped around the other and clasped in sweetnesses. Ichabod spoke out between his heartbeats that felt like pure blood spilling out into the calm, electric night, that contained a sickly-sweet sense of the uncanny, of that dream-like quality of horror at encountering in the flesh what can not be, the product of all one's nightly nightmares - the unbelief when one looks down to find the cut, the slash through shirt or jacket, lifts his fingers from the rend to see blood and internal necessities leaking from a wound - the flow of his outpouring words felt like that little death of revelation - "Rebekah shouldn't know."

"she shouldn't"

"no"

"where are we, dorris?"

"underneath the moon," they glanced up at the infinite mindless rows of lights and cameras.

"what are we doing here?"

"we're waiting."

"what?"

"for someone."

"who?"

a silence crept to their side and shushed the thin electric buzzings of the night. An echoing began, a parody of laughter.

"simon, you are going to have fun here. do you hear me, Ichabod? you're going to have fun in this place."

Ichabod turned confusedly to face her. her image blurred and slipped away from the grasp of his eyes. he coughed a capful of stinging bile back down his throat and passed his hand in front of his eyes. he slumped sickly onto the glass of the refrigerated shelf. "i don't feel so well, dorris."

"no, dear Ichabod has had a busy night. hold me, Ichabod baby."

"i feel sick. i've had a busy night."

the chemical montages of his many nightmares sunk up out of the gloom of his vision. "it's coming."

"yes. it's coming." it's coming jack, it's coming. i'm going to bite your goddamned head off. i'm going to pierce your fucking lips.

"did you say that?"

"what?"

what's happening?

we're making love.

and he realized they were. she'd undone the top buttons of her pants and pressed insistently against him against the glass and rubbing the pink flesh, parting, hard against him. she was breathing heavily and sucking at his ear, she was pressing her hand up inside her blouse and against the hard pink kernel there.

you wanna fuck me, jack? you wanna fuck me hard? make me bleed?

Dorris -

she pressed insistently.

flies buzzed around the sow's head and sucked up the dried saliva in the corner of its mouth and leapt between the crevices where blood blackened.

sweet sweet Ich, i wanna suck your blood. i wanna eat your heart out.

rebekah shouldn't know. no. she shouldn't. rebekah shouldn't know. she shouldn't. no.

a thick and turgid buzzing filled the air, pulsing louder and louder. specks swarmed in all still objects; a great rushing filled his head, a powerful gash of wind blasted across his mind and rent him, vibrating, a sounding fork image of Ichabod in twain from its colorless, corporeal doppelganger, reeling on the concrete tile spinning staring upwards glancing at the ceiling panels - a thick static filled the air and there was blood in his mouth, he lying on the floor without remembering how he got there and Dorris red-lipped sitting astraddle him with giant goddamned fangs and smiling sweetly, oh so sweetly smiling and whispering goddamned static buzzing filling the whole damn goddamned air and booming from the speaker system and kissing from her lips that sickly sweet that bitter, bitter static whispering from her lips and booming from the speaker system, little kisses of an alien tongue caressing across him like a strange saliva, “PER ME SI VA NELLA CITTA DOLENTE, ICHABOD; PER ME SI VA NELL’ ETTERNO DOLORE. PER ME SI VA TRA LA PERDUTA GENTE, LOVER” she leaned closer and ran her pointed lick that split in the middle, a gray and pebbly sort of flicking lick that tongued all over up and down his neck and ran its pebbly flesh up the length of his shoulder and settled in his ear to whisper, “want, you *want* it honey, want it - love, oooh, i *love,* honey, huuuuneeey, oooh, i *love*

Love is forever, Ichabod. Now we can be together forever. The room was red-tinged with the cheap effulgence of a scarlet wicker lampshade. He straddled her with his shirt off, she, also, with hers. She lay with her stomach pressed against the bed beneath his hands and smiled with her eyes closed. Although the morning brought silence, and the lengthening of shadows, for now the sun hung in the slow rotation of the lampshade, shaken by the stirrings on the bed.

“Happy birthday, baby,” he leaned down to press his chest against her and bring his arms to her shoulders. Into her ear, “God I’m gonna miss you.” He choked a little on his silence. “I’ll be so goddamned empty.” She opened her eyes and peered uncomfortably backwards at him.

“Hey.” He began to cry. “Hey,” she turned over and put her arms around him and he lay his head down in the circle of her warmth. “Hey, shhhhhh...” His body trembled.

“this is goddamned bullshit.“ she ran her fingers across his hair and made soft clucking, hushing sounds.

hmm... i'll need some time to think about that. although it's entirely possible that i could add more narrative handholds to this piece, in some ways that would be artificial. i conceive the movement of the poem as taking place through a series of succeeding, often dislocated images, affects, and locations - so in the beginning we have no external landscape at all, just the body (some body, anybody - the subject's body? the body of who/whatever he/she is remembering?); in the second stanza... a sliding glass door in a house overlooking a salt pan in the desert? a random pane of standing glass in the middle of the desert? in any case, a relatively surreal setting, not necessarily concretely anchored to a particular narrative; in the third stanza some kind of apocalyptic flamescape - maybe the same desert, maybe not? doesn't really matter; and finally in the last a dried up, petrified river lethe, all its blossoms turned to stone.

so really - there really is no declarative narrative, just this series of texturally linked but shifting landscapes, bursts of image and affect, a sort of succeeding linguistic texture that wants to be read as the narrative of shifting a shifting linguistic texture rather than the narrative of a particular person at a particular place remembering a particular thing.

that said, i think - in ways that preserve both the meter and the dislocated narrative - that probably something resembling declaratives do need to be teased in in places.

again - i'll think and revise.

Geez bill - it really does seem like a dodge. What you're saying doesn't seem to make sense to me. I'm saying that a particular metaphor - the tones like virgin sighs - is super cliche and needs work. By definition, a  metaphor can't be a fact in the sense you seem to be using it. Or an event. Or a thought. The poem says that the tones could have been a virgin's sighs, which if we want to be prickly about it they couldn't have.

So - tones trigger memories of sighs as the fact or truth to which you will maintain militant fidelity. Whatever, awesome. But there are many ways you could recreate that transition from tones to her sighs in the poem while still working against cliche. So in that sense I feel that you are dodging my comment about those particular lines and that particular poetic device by using the idea of "just the facts ma'am" as an excuse to avoid finding fresh ways to poetically communicate the details of your experience.

And I think it can be refreshing working within set, traditional forms - a virtuosic test of poetic mettle. if you'll notice i was inspired by the debate in this thread to write up some stanzas in sapphic meter, posted here. So more power to you (although i also value flexibility and eclecticism, and traditional forms as one tool within a formal arsenal rather than an end all be all - but nonetheless). It's as if comments that suggest chucking the meter have said, "I can't stand this movie. Why don't you try doing it on stage next time?" They aren't addressed to your poem, as such, but to the historical precedent of its form. You're working within the form, and so it seems to me that feedback -- in order to be genuinely constructive -- will attempt to help it maximize how well it's capitalizing on that form, rather than suggest that it do something contrary.

now you're the one dodging nicely, bill.

you've made "facts" into a metaphysics all their own. as if you've mapped out a total recall of your emotional, intellectual, sensory, and bodily processes during that particular moment with these few lines. did you fart? how many times did your heart beat? what were you wearing? how did the ground feel against your shoes? what other microscopic memory connections did that one thought branch out into in the milliseconds you held it?

the facts are a thin shield to hide behind. you are present as creator of this poem at the very least in the capacity of selecting the precise elements from the absolutely massive experiential database of just that moment that you have to draw from. so select something from that database that's not a flaccid cliche like music as virgin sighs. if you're so concerned about material fact, why not shy away from language and metaphors that are so rutted, overused, and therefore *abstracted from* "factness" and the immediacy of your material reality and the linear narration of events as to be little more than linguistic refuse.

So I have twice now composed and deleted an agonizingly composed response on my phone. I had to turn on the laptop and type it up there before I broke something.

CS – I know sweet fuck-all about ragweed. Not that it matters in terms of how well the poem accomplishes “sincerity,” but on this rare occasion I did happen to be writing about my daughter, rather than something made up (not that I’m writing about her in a sincere way or using images or language that are precisely accurate or whatever – no rag purple dress, for example).

Just so you know, I’m not being a smartass by asking for examples of sincerity – I tend to associate sincerity in verse with a pretty particular kind of poetics, especially the new American poetry and the beats, and so some clarifications as to the particular registers you want to capture by appealing to sincerity would help me better orient myself to your comment (and that whole appeal probably just made me seem like even more of a smartass – bringing us right back to the role of language in creating the semblance of sincerity).

But I see and agree that ragweed – as I’m guessing it’s a particularly yucky kind of weed? – doesn’t work as a title (I was just going for the convergence of weeds and the association with the rag dress). Alternative suggestions?

Thanks for taking the time CS, I appreciate your feedback.

Rg – which part of the hair thing? Mojave seems to be saying that the love-burnt wheat stalks crap is working, but it needs to be toned down after that.

Thanks for the feedback

Mojave: the problem is that I don’t want the image of the little girl to be balanced by the reality of a child’s life. I want the little girl in the poem absorbed by image, such that we’re tracing along the surface of bright weeds as little girls.

If I were going to take the advice to tone down the rest, I might be more inclined just to chop it after the first two lines, and skip right to “in time to come.”

or to the rag purple dress as a milkthistle flower (cs - I Googled that one first)

As to the final lines, I have to admit to a sort of shameful sympathy for maudlin sentimentality, in my weak moments. I had hoped that the dense images of the first part, along with the heavy theological sentiments of the second, might carve out a little space for the (admittedly) sappy “remember me / little flower” to sneak in.

How do others feel about the last two lines?

So in any case, Mojave, how do you feel about the following (either as a poem complete or as a unit to build on):

milkthistle

my little girl’s hair like

love-burnt stalks, and the rag-

purple dress, her glory.

in time to come there will be no

weeds, but bodies of light and power.

Thanks all for the time and feedback,

matt

One of the biggest problems I’m having with this piece is the diffusion of its images. Many seem to have nothing to do with each other. For example, I suppose I can go for chocolate to piccolo – music and food, aesthetic consumption, going along with these little sacrifices – but from that to Philadelphia? and the recycling plants? and what in the world does their dislike of the color of Amish horse wagons have to do with anything? And how does all of this proceed from Samurai? (I like this image a great deal, but its register is disjointed from all that comes after)

I admit completely the possibility that I as a reader have simply missed something completely obvious and vital to the poem. But as it stands yr images need much more … unity of register. we’re all over the place here.

I was struck by this disjoint in register in the following lines:

Many live

in Philadelphia and do not have first names.

They smell of New York Times stacked

at recycling plants; (although this one could end up working, I’m not sure yet)

They dislike the color of Amish horse wagons,

but fly-out wilding at dusk into the heavens;

I thought the first lines of stanza three is where the qualities that are jarring with my reading become most obvious in terms of unity of register. The language of the second line of stanza three is particularly vague, and “heavens” is more weight than the line can bear.

the little birds a samurais is wonderful (even though it doesn’t seem to fit with the rest). “their bright eyes burn yellow as yard lights” imho, is brilliant, along with “gods implacable and cruel as our own” (although I think the preceding “melancholic” is not the right word, a bit too heavy and latinate, especially since where you really want that slightly abstracting heaviness is not at “melancholic” but rather at “implacable and cruel” – so I would save it for there.

I would argue that “bright eyes yellow as yard lights” captures where the thematic energy of the poem is at its strongest, in this convergence of this sortof sickly force of nature in the figure of the birds that is both pedestrian and unremarkable and distasteful and at the same time wild and pagan and a little bit sublime.

I think that the second to last line bears a lot of weight in the poem, and I’d urge you to tweak it slightly. but again my suggestion here might be guided by a misunderstanding of some basic narrative feature of the poem. what about having them flying into windows and breaking their necks?

p\. s. my last post in poem a day (with the ridiculously long title) was written with you in mind. give it a read.

**[The Poetic AX ~ Sharp Critique](http://www.tinroofalleypoets.org/poetry_boards/index.php/board,57.0.html) / [Re: it's america \> right](http://www.tinroofalleypoets.org/poetry_boards/index.php/topic,16885.msg124902.html#msg124902)**

Cy, (I hate this bastard phone and trying to type on it - in sum, I'd strongly suggest dropping the task and repeated it's America, right - they don't accomplish annything that the poem doesn't already accomplish in subtler and more skillful ways)

This piece is lyrical and almost minimalist. I enjoy it very much.

On the one hand, this lyrical quality is central to the poetics of this piece. The almost sing-song repetitions, the chorus-like quality of the recurrence of certain words, like rosemary. And you achieve a kind of trimmed down purity of language that fits the poem's subject. The sing-song poetics are almost--but not quite--the voice of the central character--who after all "bites \[his\] tongue," but seem to arise out of the mutual dance of aestheticizing deception created by both characters. Most poignant and subtly tragic--more world weary and melancholic than tragic, I guess--is the awareness of the poem and its characters of their deception  in combination with an unwillingness or inability to do anything about it. The poem tells you its sing-song isn't real ("pretend again and again"), and invites the reader to be lured in and ensorcelled by its seduction.

That said, I felt that the repeated use of ya and it's America / right were overkill. We don't need them for the poem's lyricism, nor do we need them to understand its characters

there was too much going on in this poem, for me.

we start with a flower, followed by a military formation of eyes, and then she’s a disease infecting them, and then out of nowhere she falls in love (does she fall in love with one of the eyes? are they bees to her flower?  and if so why does the eyes or people or bees then transform into an evaporating raindrop?)

and then something’s eating at her (are they little plant/flower parasites? antibiotics because she’s a disease?)

and then she’s a flame, which leads me to believe the eyes or people or bees or raindrops have now transformed into moths (attracted by the her light, because she’s now a candle or a lamp?)

but they aren’t even attracted to the fire because she’s a ruin (not a word I’d use to describe a flower – although:

the ruins of a flower could actually be an interesting image)

but she’s not a candle or a lamp she’s napalm, and the followers she’s deterring now aren’t eyes or people or bees or moths anymore (unless she’s just going way overboard with the napalm and the moths. I guess that is one way to fix a bug problem)

also, I think you could productively replace some of the poem’s abstractions with more concrete images, as for example

elegant

aura

love

perfection

forever

finite

open heart

unconventional moments

innocence

memories

sweetness

trust

So:

 

1)I understand you might not want or need to maintain a single metaphor throughout the poem, but as it stands it feels too cluttered for me, and

2\) the poem, for me and as it stands, is carried by far too many abstractions and empty generalities.

forgive if I’ve been harsh. I like tiny upturned corners of the mouth, and the baptism in rain, and a number of things. I even like some the things the seem to draw the poem in too many directions, as for example the phalanx of bees or whatever.

hope that helps,

forgive me if not,

matt

**400**

**[The Poetic AX ~ Sharp Critique](http://www.tinroofalleypoets.org/poetry_boards/index.php/board,57.0.html) / [across a dewclaw crystal set](http://www.tinroofalleypoets.org/poetry_boards/index.php/topic,16918.msg125122.html#msg125122)**

« **on:** April 24, 2012, 10:28 AM »

across a dewclaw crystal set

the moon transmits in tongues,

shadows pinned to a wall

memories of Waycross

hospital's sanitized bed,

her hands like interlocking

sawtooth flowers.

after the service, the sun

broadcasting beastangel,

the waves a clanging acoustic Baboon

i spread her ashes on the water

in cursive herons,

worm-carved index cards like strawberries

or wild babies.\*

\*This poem expresses personal and emotional feelings. They are not invented or exaggerated. I am the author of this poem. I created all the words and sentences that make up this poem. This is a poem about a day on the ocean. I am the subject of this poem and all of the experiences in this poem are real. This footnote is not a part of the poem and its role is purely to help my reader understand my experiences and emotions. All of the images and events that I relate in this poem make logical and contextual sense. They are transparent and easily understood. The purpose of my poem is communication.

The following is a description of the real events and emotions that I express in my poem.

Stanza 1 (one):

The moon sent a message on a crystal radio set. This is not a personification. The crystal radio set was constructed entirely of dewclaws, a kind of vestigial finger or toe. The message was made of shadows. The moon related it in tongues or *glossolalia*, because it is Pentecostal.

Stanza 2 (two):

The shadows were a memory. The moon transmitted them to me. I remembered the night my mother died at Waycross hospital, in Waycross, Pennsylvania. My mother is not currently alive and Waycross, Pennsylvania is not a made-up town.

Stanza 3 (three):

I remembered this on the day of my mother’s funeral, after the service. I was on a boat. It was a hot day. Each ocean wave was simultaneously a Baboon. This is not a metaphor. Each Baboon had a cymbal, which he clanged. The Baboons did not have electric amplifiers for their cymbals.

Stanza 4 (four):

As I remembered, I was spreading my mother’s ashes on the Baboons. I spread them in cursive herons, a phrase which can have at least two meanings: 1) as I spread the ashes, they formed the shape of herons, as in “I spread my coins in a row;” or 2) I poured the ashes into the bodies of herons. Both meanings are true. The herons were not printed herons, but cursive ones.

The final two lines are self-explanatory.

[**Quote from: illiterati on April 24, 2012, 10:28 AM**](http://www.tinroofalleypoets.org/poetry_boards/index.php/topic,16918.msg125122.html#msg125122)

across a dewclaw crystal set

the heat-maddened moon transmits

murmurs in a thousand tongues, shadows

pinned to the wall in a cave

memory tomb: the brink

can grow bright:

the swollen lights at Waycross hospital.

the sanitized bed, her hands like

interlocking sawtooth flowers.

angelus sun

broadcasts beastangel, clanging acoustic Baboon:

her ashes scrawled on curls of waves

a life streaming out like

cursive herons

the hullabaloo sends

abstruse envelope blondness

and worm-carved index cards

soft like strawberries or wild babies.

**Quote from: illiterati**

across a dewclaw crystal set

the heat-maddened moon transmits in night-time tongues

that murmur in a thousand unheard languages like shadows

pinned to the wall in a cave,

memory tomb a legacy of veins. the brink

can grow bright:

the swollen toy lights at Waycross hospital

at dusk. in the hospital bed, hands like interlocking

sawtooth flowers.

angelus sun broadcasts in beastangel

knells like small breathers clanging acoustic Baboon:

her ashes to dark curls of waves

a red life streaming out with the ragged

purity of herons

the congestive hullabaloo sends

in effigies of abstruse envelope blondness

worm-carved index cards like

strawberries or wild babies.

it's terrible, i know. you'd think with all the plants.... but no. i'm lucky to identify a dandelion.

as to the poem - i'm putting the poem up to receive feedback about the poem as a poem, not about the poem as an extension of my emotional life. i have other people i go to receive feedback on my emotional life.

why do people keep writing poems about the same old sappy stuff?

(because we're all hoping they'll put the language together in a way that makes it new)

what separates hannah montanna's diary entry from a poignant poem?

(the language and form that construct it - that's the poem qua poem)

so you might as well ask any writer why they're writing when they could just be saying.

"i feel sad"

"someone's mother died and she spread her ashes on the sea"

and now that's taken care of.

or maybe this is not a question of language and form but of emotional maturity or sincerity?

i know many wise and emotionally mature people who would make terrible poets.

and many immature and unwise people who make great poets.

and to what degree is emotion and perception itself a poem? a self-dialogue constructed with language and biochemical meters?

and anyways now the poem does say something.

it's a narrative about a crystal set radio made out of dewclaws (a vestigial digit on the foot of many mammals)

that broadcasts to the subject of the poem a memory of a hospital room and his or her dying mother

while in the present he and/or she is spreading his or her mother's ashes on the sea.

and those spreading ashes look like cursive herons and worm-carved index cards

which in turn look like strawberries or wild babies.

simple.

so you see i am saying something, regardless of the process behind it.

so how about those modifiers? less cluttered? specific suggestions about the language or form of the poem?

sure, let's start over.

if what you're going for was a poem as "expression," this failed, at least to my reading. I could make no sense of it.

but i wasn't reading the poem as an attempt to say something, but rather as an interesting artifact of language.

i was most intrigued by the way that the poem seemed to shift between distinct "voices"

there is a gnomic voice, steeped in abstruse symbolism (or at least what appears to be abstruse symbolism):

"rearranged destiny / with a cat and a broomstick" (that's my favorite)

and then a sort of diaristic voice that sounds like a speaker reporting events/feelings:

"It was something sickly, edging on love" \[i really like this line, by the way"

"I met him in Londontown"

so that's the (at least two) voices i hear in the poem.

thematically the poem seems to be really invested in different ideas of voice, distinct speakers and ways of speaking / making sounds / etc.:

"insists the tedious voice of count"

"malicious demons interrupt"

"humming a smoky Adele melody"

I like this aspect of the poem's language, and think you could make it stronger by emphasizing the distinctness of the various voices or modes of speech in the poem, their difference from each other in the way they speak and what they want to speak about.

i really didn't put any thought into how to do this, except the very basic conceit of putting "taste his madness on your tongue" in quotation marks. (the demons speaking?)

seraph:

thanks for your time. sure, there's janus and the moth, and then there's the more readily available association of the moth with... a sort of self-destructive desire for forbidden knowledge, summarized in the phrase "the moth and the flame." this is a phrase and idea that should be available to most people, regardless of grounding in a literary tradition, on the simple basis of the bug zapper; as well as having the deeper resonances of ecstatic mystical knowledge - "the moth and the flame" is a common metaphor for the self-consuming drive of the mystic towards union with the divine other - god as the flame that promises a form of annihilation to the contemplative, and which the contemplative can nonetheless not resist throwing herself towards with abandon.

mojave:

in this, instance, i feel it incumbent upon myself to offer a brief defense of this exercise and its style.

offering a quoted sentence here won't dissuade me: i have my own sentences in mind.

so first of all, what i believe you are labeling "mere rescitation like a well drilled schoolboy repeating facts" is classic Gertrude Stein. I couldn't help but hearing her sentences from "Melanctha" in *Three Lives* as I was writing this, for a number of reasons. my counter-quote, first:

**Quote from: gertrude stein**

The men would call out, “Say, Sis, look out or we’ll come and catch yer,” or “Hi, there, you yaller girl, come here and we’ll take you saillin’.” And then, too, Melanctha would learn to know some of the serious foreign sailors who told her all sorts of wonders, and a cook would sometimes take her and her friends over a ship and show where he made his messes and where the men slept, and where the shops were, and how everything was made by themselves, right there, on ship board.     98

  Melanctha loved to see these dark and smelly places. She always loved to watch and talk and listen with men who worked hard. But it was never from these rougher people that Melanctha tried to learn the ways that lead to wisdom. In the daylight she always liked to talk with rough men and to listen to their lives and about their work and their various ways of doing, but when the darkness covered everything all over, Melanctha would meet, and stand, and talk with a clerk or a young shipping agent who had seen her watching, and so it was that she would try to learn to understand.

so the repetitiveness and sort of heavy (but sing-songy) use of the past progressive that i make use of in sentences like "He was always lying with Gomer, always wanting to know and see the secret moths he found in her. He was always feeling on the verge of knowing the symbols bitten into Gomer’s tablets." is pretty much straight Stein.

also steinian is the use of this simplistic / repetitive diction in the context of a narrative about forbidden knowledge, and the link between sexual and social knowledge very much owes a debt to stein's melanctha.

but my more immediate intertext is anne carson's "the book of isaiah." she uses shorter sentences, and her narrative is in many ways more invested in rewriting the biblical narrative than mine is, but i was most thinking of her when it comes to the dense and resistant "anti-symbols" and opaque poetic language of the piece.

so for example, carson uses language such as:

**Quote from: anne carson**

The nation stirred in its husk and slept again.

Two slabs of bloody meat lay folded on its eyes like wings.   

\*

Inside Isaiah God saw the worldsheet burning.

\*

Yet I have invented sin, thought Isaiah, running his hand over the knobs.

\*

God washed Isaiah’s hair in fire.

in fact - this is the main reason i felt in this instance compelled to defend the poetic language of the piece.

the very fact that, in your response to "moths" you ask for some kind of relatable image (what would he do with the moths?) troubles me.

have you looked at the images in the poem? they are consistently and willfully resistant to being reduced to... metaphors. to some kind of transparent symbol through which we glimpse a deeper meaning. in fact, i'd be willing to say that all of the poetic language in the piece is consciously anti-metaphorical:

staining himself with reptile feathers

curious sensation of moths... in his throat

the symbols bitten into Gomer's tablets

they carved his eyes with burning water

lowered her veil of antlers

expressionless as ceramic lipstick

\*

not a one of these instances of language can be reduced to... a clear image. a transparent metaphor.

if they are a symbol for anything, it's the obduracy of whatever forbidden knowledge hosea is seeking. this knowledge--whatever the moths are whispering-- *can't* enter into language as a direct symbol or metaphor.

it's very much the forbidden knowledge that hosea is pursuing that shows up in the poem's language... as a sort of *perversion* of metaphor and symbol.

\*

also just a quick point: you've got the biblical narrative backwards. not that i think you need the biblical narrative to know that this piece isn't about the redemption of Gomer, but if you're going to refer to the poem's most obvious intertext you should be clear about its point.

the OT book of Hosea is specifically NOT about the redemption of Gomer. God commands Hosea to marry the prostitute Gomer so that he will be initiated into the UNredemption of the faithless prostitute as a figure for the faithless israel:

1:2 When the Lord first spoke through  Hosea, he said to him,  “Go marry  a prostitute who will bear illegitimate children conceived through prostitution,  because the nation continually commits spiritual prostitution by turning away from the Lord.”

 just look at the names of their children:

\*\*“Name him ‘Jezreel,’ because in a little while I will punish the dynasty of Jehu on account of the bloodshed in the valley of Jezreel, and I will put an end to the kingdom of Israel.

\*\*“Name her ‘No Pity’ (Lo-Ruhamah) because I will no longer have pity on the nation of Israel. For I will certainly not forgive their guilt.

etc.

so, although there is some vague promise of a future redemption for israel, the whole point of the prophet marrying the prostitue is his initiation into god's own suffering, chaining the prophet to a sort of impossible love and desire for an unredeemable object.

and in this poem it's become a narrative of hosea's fascination with forbidden knowledge, simultaneously a figure for the erotics of mystical knowledge: it is, after all, the holiest of holies, with its countless veils seraphim wings, that hosea finds underneath gomer's veil of antlers.

maybe the humming noise should shout out "holy"?

\*

and one more (i must be stupidly verbose today):

mojave, can you *really* not find any symbolic significance in foot washing in the context of a rewrite of a biblical narrative?

thanks as always for your attention to this piece. details are the most helpful.

again, i know that your advice will probably lead to much better "expressive" poems, and probably more publishable poems, too.

but i also want to practice anti-expressive and slightly antagonistic poetics.

how to do both?

praise?!

on the other hand, i feel like this poem has completely failed. many of these images were meant to come off as surreal bordering on farcical. and the footnote - which is a new addition i don't think anyone has read - was added as a way to underscore the fact that the poem is not sincere.

here is what i have decided to do:

the other poem will be a version that - as much as i'm able to do - is utterly impossible to read as sincere or poignant. whose images announce themselves as willfully impossible and out-of-place and obtuse.

so - i'll be chewing away at both versions.

thanks very much to everyone for your time and feedback.

I do remember, but I thought you weren't intending the footnote as a part of your poem. It was something external to the poem - a device meant to help orient your reader to the historical context of the poem.

Whereas my footnotes are farce that participate in the aesthetic world of the poem itself.

i'm sure that many people disagreed with the so-called "consensus" about footnotes. i certainly did - you make a good point about the wasteland.

although - again i think this is an important distinction, whether the footnote is meant to be or functions as something outside the world of the poem - a narrator poking in from without to tell you what the poem means and how to read it.

or whether the footnote functions as an aspect of the voice of the poem itself. something included in its imaginary world and engaged in creating its aesthetics.

despite their presentation as "scholarly" addendum to eliot's abstruse poem, i would argue that the footnotes to the wasteland are the latter, rather than the former: part of the aesthetic world of the poem. the poem would not be the same poem without those footnotes.

just like eliot's conceit of numbering his own lines, the footnotes to the wasteland participate in a kind of self-canonization of the poem, and signal the peculiarly modern development of disciplinary knowledge that mediates our access to "poems" - the footnotes signal the ways in which various kinds of academic disciplines have come to be a central part of how we access and understand poetry.

and of course there's the most obvious function of the footnotes as cementing the poem's hyper-erudition and allusiveness. the footnotes guarantee the poem's cultural capital.

so really, it seems to me that the wasteland's footnotes are an important part of its poetics.

**[The Poetic AX ~ Sharp Critique](http://www.tinroofalleypoets.org/poetry_boards/index.php/board,57.0.html) / [Sonnet Written by Computer Brain](http://www.tinroofalleypoets.org/poetry_boards/index.php/topic,16918.msg125424.html#msg125424)**

here is the first half of the dewclaw rewrite -- this is the version that's supposed to make sense, so have at it.

and the footnote is not a footnote: it's part of the poem. please feel free to make suggestions for the language etc. of the footnote as well.

(and Bill: here's a sonnet for you. i welcome your insights.)

Sonnet Written by Computer Brain

“the names of dust”

the moon pins shadows to the wall, each night

transmitting tongues of angels, static songs

which i with my ancient crystal set record

because, though dark, i sometimes see

in otherwise faint symbols, uncanny bursts of sense:

like here, this yellow notebook, hidden deep

in opaque letters, an image in ascending rows:

my mother’s fingers, resting on the rail

of waycross hospital bed, like interlocking

sawtooth flowers. or here, this starburst spread:

her ashes fanning out through ocean, worm-

carved arcs through dirt. thrust down through rarified air

and space: the voice i find each night at dusk

my solemn archive of the names of dust.\*

\*“Poem Written by Computer”

The real achievement,” reported researchers, “is in what we haven’t programmed: we’ve constructed parameters for the self-directed development and evolution of the program’s code. In other words, this is a computer that learns.

After a certain amount of data collection, the computer is designed to rewrite its own programming and adapt in response to statistical algorithms that measure the potential success of its verse.

It starts with randomized combinations of words and letters. It's plugged into a database of English language sonnets, which it then scrambles and recombines. PAL can write about 6000 sonnets per second. At that rate, it's been learning how to put a pretty good poem together.

We’re just at the beta stage, at the moment, but we’re more than pleased with the results we’ve produced even with these rudiments of the ultimate project. The next thing that will be up and running is the concrete poetry generator. Eventually, we hope to get to the point where the program can compose in any medium, including blank verse, and understand the abstract relationships between its poems well enough to put together chapbooks and short collections. But that's a long way off."

[**Quote from: illiterati on April 24, 2012, 10:28 AM**](http://www.tinroofalleypoets.org/poetry_boards/index.php/topic,16918.msg125122.html#msg125122)

across a dewclaw crystal set

the moon transmits in tongues,

shadows pinned to a wall

memories of Waycross

hospital's sanitized bed,

her hands like interlocking

sawtooth flowers.

after the service, the sun

broadcasting beastangel,

the waves a clanging acoustic Baboon

i spread her ashes on the water

in cursive herons,

worm-carved index cards like strawberries

or wild babies.\*

\*This poem expresses personal and emotional feelings. They are not invented or exaggerated. I am the author of this poem. I created all the words and sentences that make up this poem. This is a poem about a day on the ocean. I am the subject of this poem and all of the experiences in this poem are real. This footnote is not a part of the poem and its role is purely to help my reader understand my experiences and emotions. All of the images and events that I relate in this poem make logical and contextual sense. They are transparent and easily understood. The purpose of my poem is communication.

The following is a description of the real events and emotions that I express in my poem.

Stanza 1 (one):

The moon sent a message on a crystal radio set. This is not a personification. The crystal radio set was constructed entirely of dewclaws, a kind of vestigial finger or toe. The message was made of shadows. The moon related it in tongues or *glossolalia*, because it is Pentecostal.

Stanza 2 (two):

The shadows were a memory. The moon transmitted them to me. I remembered the night my mother died at Waycross hospital, in Waycross, Pennsylvania. My mother is not currently alive and Waycross, Pennsylvania is not a made-up town.

Stanza 3 (three):

I remembered this on the day of my mother’s funeral, after the service. I was on a boat. It was a hot day. Each ocean wave was simultaneously a Baboon. This is not a metaphor. Each Baboon had a cymbal, which he clanged. The Baboons did not have electric amplifiers for their cymbals.

Stanza 4 (four):

As I remembered, I was spreading my mother’s ashes on the Baboons. I spread them in cursive herons, a phrase which can have at least two meanings: 1) as I spread the ashes, they formed the shape of herons, as in “I spread my coins in a row;” or 2) I poured the ashes into the bodies of herons. Both meanings are true. The herons were not printed herons, but cursive ones.

The final two lines are self-explanatory.

bill - so glad you didn't decide to withhold your voice from the ax.

some people prefer complexity.

i prefer complexity when reading poetry. sometimes i even prefer nonsense.

*detailed responses v. general discussions about poetics*

first of all, i'd like to be very clear about something:

my verbosity in defense of this particular poem is in response to a lack of details in mojave's reply.

there's nothing wrong with his lack of specific, linguistic comments about this poem, but from the beginning it was not a discussion about this poem per se.

this is a general discussion about poetics, style, school, method, etc.

as you'll see when reading through other posts, i've been quite responsive to *specific and detailed* feedback.

but what can i do with - "this style doesn't work, here's a sentence from so-and-so"?

again - this kind of feedback is a wonderful occasion for a lively discussion about poetics in general

but not so much in terms of revising my poem - thus, the discussion above.

\*

*referring to outside texts and interpretation*

as i've pointed out, i don't think any knowledge of "hosea" is necessary to approach this poem.

the point i've been trying to make, in response to mojave, is that there's no good reason to dismiss this poem as a "fallen woman" narrative out-of-hand simply by referring to the original text.

and interpretation isn't solely in the eyes of the beholder. yes, there is a personal element. yes, differing interpretations can be equally intelligent, well-reasoned, and plausible.

but i think we would all agree that the primary theme of shakespeare's sonnets is not the erotic trauma of alien abduction.

mojave quoted that passage as "proof" that hosea is about the redemption of gomer.

but there's nothing in that passage about the redemption of gomer.\*

so whether that's in the passage or not is *not* in the eye of the beholder. it's just not there.

*the ethics of critting:*

for me, there are ethical issues at stake in responding to and critiquing a poem:

when i approach a poem, my job is not to force my own poetic sensibilities and values on it.

because i know my own perspective and values are limited, i attempt to **approach the other poem on its own terms, as much as possible.**

so for example, bill -- i understand that my investment in experimentalism is limited.

therefore i don't approach poems i'm responding to on the basis of how experimental they are -- unless that is what they're trying to achieve.

as much as possible, i attempt to look at the poem on its own terms and from that perspective offer whatever i can to help the poem achieve what it sets out to achieve.

clarity, as a poetic value, bill, is a pretty limited and particular kind of value.

which i can respect, and even try to adopt when responding to poems that want to achieve it.

and even try to practice myself on occasion! i spent days laboring over the "ragweed" post -- clarity, sincerity, image: these are not easy for me. and eventually i came up with a rewrite that, as far as i can tell, much more fully represents those values.

but when i'm writing a poem like this, whose purpose would clearly be undone by striving for "clear" metaphors-- i really can't respond in detail to comments that suggest i abandon this.

that's not the poem i'm trying to write.

in the same spirit, bill, i would not respond to a sonnet of yours by suggesting that you ditch iambic pentameter, even though iambic pentameter isn't a form i prefer to work in.

because that would make absolutely no sense for a poem that wants to be a sonnet -

and not just any sonnet, but a sonnet that exhibits clarity, precision, a grounding in "actual" events and feelings and thoughts and memories.

fine - i will try to approach your poem on those terms.

so i would just like to emphasize that i'm not "denigrat\[ing\] the insights of others based on \[my\] vision"

but in response to the (prescriptive, judgmental, and pretty much evangelistic) general sentiment that there is no place in the world of verse for obduracy, and difficulty (not that this is mojave's position vis a vis difficulty in verse - but it might be yours), i think it's fine to respond as forcefully as i'm able

to assert the right of experimentalism to exist.

now - if we'd like to talk about how well this particular poem achieves those goals, i'm sure there are many failures and weaknesses about which we could together brainstorm how to improve

\*\*

and bill, really:

my education or lack thereof has nothing to do with the current discussion.

what are you, running for office?

try to respond to the content of what we're talking about, here

shifting the responsibility of your response onto my education,

rather than what i've said

is what we call a dodge.

\*(he does "buy her back" in the most literal sense of shelling out some shekels, but there just isn't anything in that passage about redemption in the spiritual or moral or social or personal sense.)

so - i regret that we will be spending so much time discussing interpretation of the original text. it's not imperative for the poem itself. in fact i'm entirely unclear how whether the biblical narrative is about the redemption of gomer or not has any bearing for or against the poem above, on its own terms.

but since the idea that the biblical narrative is about the redemption of gomer has, for you mojave, become a point against the poem, i do have to again express my deep and profound confusion about how you are reading the redemption of gomer from the passage you quote. gomer is a temple prostitute in the passage you quote, and throughout the book of hosea. there's no redemption. the point of the narrative is not the redemption of gomer, but rather about hosea's initiation into god's suffering. hosea will learn what it feels like to desire a faithless lover. that's the point. it's not about the redemption of gomer. there's no way you can get "the redemption of gomer" from what you're quoting.

this is a frivolous point, one way or the other, because:

gomer is not important in the poem. again - you will have to explain to me how the fact that the original text is a "fallen woman" narrative, as you call it, has anything to do with the narrative of this poem, which is clearly focused on hosea's desire for forbidden knowledge. gomer isn't really a character in the piece at all, more like a statue. she is expressionless, she wears her veil of antlers, she's got the ceramic lipstick thing going on - she's the "objective correlative" - no more. not an actual character that draws our emotional engagement one way or another.

and again, i'm not sure what you're specifying when you say i can't have it both ways. the biblical narrative isn't pristine, neither is the poetic rewrite. the foot washing is sexual - but it is sexual precisely because it's asexual. the narrative leads us to expect sex - it talks about shamelessness in the first line, and then moves to...

foot-washing. it *sublates* the sexual energy we're led to expect into the asexual foot washing. it would have been equally sexualized if i had written any number of things:

In the marriage bed, Hosea was at first excited by Gomer's shamelessness.

He was always trimming and trimming her nails.

OR

He was always polishing and polishing her veil of antlers.

OR whatever  - the point is that the foot washing becomes sexualized only because of its narrative context - we're lead to expect sexual, and so the foot washing is sexual. anything that went there would have had the same significance. anything that went there would have become a perverse transfer of sexual energy into some other act or object. that's the point.

again, as we see with the obtuse metaphors, the point is the way the forbidden and impossible knowledge enters into language as a sort of linguistic perversion.

we'll call that reptile feathers.

\*

and you know, honestly, i'm sure that i'd be happier if this piece could match stein's experimentalism *and* her tenderness to alice. perhaps i'll give it a shot.

but this piece is not that. how could this piece be written as tenderness towards an object of affection?

he was always caring for and thinking about her reptile feathers?

he was always polishing and cleaning her antler veil?

i'm just not sure how it would be done.

\*

and as to the carson - yes, anne's language is beautiful, more so than stein's in the passage i quote.

but i quoted anne for the obduracy and inappropriateness of her metaphors as a response to your quip about the moths and the inappropriateness of the poem's metaphors / inability to link them with some kind of real life comparison.

the point of the carson was, i'm modeling my images off the way she creates images in the quote.

as slabs of meat on eyes like wings doesn't make sense as a clear image or metaphor,

neither do moths in a throat, or symbols bitten into tablets, or carving eyes with burning water.

i'm striving for a metaphorical principle similar to anne's in the quoted passage.

\*

I think the rules that govern what goes where in terms of columns need to be much more explicit.

so either: all the austere ocean description in one column,

and all the degraded domestic scenes in another

or: all the decent poetry in one column,

and obviously corny / bad poetry in the other (you’d have to emphasize its badness)

and then if you’re going to break up the consistency of the columns, wait until later in the poem so that the muddling/intermixing of the column’s language can reflect some development in theme or something. as it stands, the columns, to my mind, seem random, unmotivated, a merely formal gimmick (and you know how I can’t stand formal gimmicks.)

(i hadn't intended the right-aligned stanzas to be so far over: i had much closer to the left hand column in mind, but right aligned rather than center)

I live above the ocean,

above the ocean’s copper

surface of debris.

The ocean has gotten out of bed      

the aberrant water talks to itself

and breathes into its own mouth

recovering its health

   

I drink. Two-fingers of gin

in a water glass.

Margaret in her yellow robe,

breasts full as gladiola,

a scent of ocean minerals.

A sea lion rests on a rock,          

honking, honking, honking.

      

The stench of day old asparagus,

her warming half-glass of tomato juice

and a Dorothy Perkins rose

in the littered sink.

Swimmers move from shore,          

buoyant, chalked with sea water       

and tinted green as lamp shades.

      

Bathroom towels move on their own

in an ocean draft.

The unruly ocean             

drifts and piles itself             

toward the clairvoyant moon.   

   

I could mimic Margaret’s speech

spoken through a half-rolled

taxi window,

her rinsed and uncombed hair

drying on the air.

I. “Poems Written by Computer Make History”

PAL (Poetry Analogue Lineator) is like no poet you've ever met.

In fact, PAL isn't even human.

"The real achievement,” reported researchers, “is in what we haven’t programmed. We designed PAL to actively participate in writing *his own code*, adapting his "art" \[laughter\] in response to statistical algorithms that measure the potential success of his verse."

PAL's "creative process" all starts with randomized combinations of words and letters. He is plugged into a database of English language sonnets, which he scrambles and recombines at incredible speeds: "PAL can write about 6000 sonnets per second," the scientists explained. "At that rate, he's been learning quickly. Right now we’re just at the beta stage of development. Eventually, we hope to get to the point where PAL can compose in any medium, including blank verse, and understand the abstract relationships between his poems well enough to put together chapbooks and short collections. But we're a long way off from realizing his full market potential.

In the meantime, we're more than pleased that PAL can crank off poems like these."

"sonnet \#1.6231 x 10^18"

by PAL

the moon pins shadows to the wall, each night

transmitting tongues of angels, static songs

which i with my ancient crystal set record

because, though dark, i sometimes see

in otherwise faint symbols, uncanny bursts of sense:

like here, this yellow notebook, hidden deep

in opaque letters, an image in ascending rows:

my mother’s fingers, resting on the rail

of waycross hospital bed, like interlocking

sawtooth flowers. or here, this starburst spread:

her ashes fanning out through ocean, worm-

carved arcs through dirt. thrust down through rarified air

and space: the voice i find each night at dusk

my solemn archive of the names of dust.

II\. "Sentimental Confessions"

Dear Reader,

The poem you will soon read expresses personal and deeply emotional feelings. In airy words I have set down the secret heart, that which was never writ on fleshy face.

Before you read, I wish to stress the nature of the passionate emotions and events herein: they are in no way invented or exaggerated. These are the facts--the heights and depths of feeling--as I have experienced them. As much as possible, I have ensured that all of the images and events that I relate in this poem are "as windows unto the world of sense," and that they are transparent and in every way understandable.

May our souls meet in poetry.

Yours,

A Hopeless Dreamer

"mourning song: a threnody"

by A Hopeless Dreamer

“I have spread my dreams under your feet,

Tread softly because you tread on my dreams”
