Tiny Studies

(Particle 3)

By Kathleen Balma

 

1.       \_\_\_\_\_\_ anorexia                a. Islands make mini species.

2.       \_\_\_\_\_\_ dementia               b. The mind is an isle of small thoughts.

3.       \_\_\_\_\_\_ insular dwarfism     c. The brain consumes itself and is lighter.

\*

The Causes of Cyclone Formation Aren't Well Understood

By Kathleen Balma

 

1

Yes, it’s true: stunted hicks are our only fruit. They grow in rows like crops and come in various shades of redneck. (Scarlet O’Scarecrow is my favorite.)

 

2

The breeze here gets so sick of us all, it spins puke-colored cumuli. Then it tunnels out these funnel clouds and impulse shops like a Tilt-O-Whirl all over our broke town, sprouting yard sales where none had grown before.

 

3

An oak fought bravely, but died defending its plot. Surviving it are four small children, dog and aunt.

 

4

What I remember seeing: the twirling wind ate the middles of things, left neat rows of rooftops for blocks and blocks. Somewhere in all this mess is my baton.

 

5

To the cellar! No cellar? Down a basement! No basement? Under stairs! No stairs? In a bathtub! No bathtub? Find a ditch! No ditch? Tag: you’re a witch!

 

6

The reason Wizard of Oz works as a film is because so few see midlands as anything but a place for flight, and even a winged grudge monkey has more social cachet than a farmer.

 

7

A weather man is an elemental wiz. As such, he can do nothing but try to predict what air already knows, then instruct you to use the dead’s shoes to find a way home.

Kathleen Balma earned an MFA in poetry from Indiana University. She is a recent Fulbright Fellow and Pushcart Prize nominee. Her poems have appeared in Atlanta Review, Crab Orchard Review, Mid-American Review, Puerto del Sol, Rattle, Salamander, and various other magazines. She is currently pursuing a doctorate in comparative literature at the University of Connecticut.

Footnotes to a History of the Beloved

By Kristina Marie Darling

 

1\. Three of the darkest flowers, which were pressed in a book and displayed on a lavish mahogany nightstand.

2\. Only then did she describe the recurring dream, in which his luminous cufflinks gave rise to a series of house fires.

3\. "I had wanted to preserve the cold white light that shone that evening. But beneath every door, a little wisp of smoke. The hallway smolders and now my armoire burning in a locked room."

4\. Violence.

1\. The use of physical coercion.

†2. The relative strength or duration of an emotion.

‡3. An unpleasant or destructive natural force.

5\. The unpublished portion of their correspondence, which documents her pilgrimage to the shrine of Saint Jude. Despite numerous appeals to divine providence, the lock of hair never appeared beneath her window.

6\. Parure. Translated from the French as ornament or embellishment.

7\. She told her sisters he had given her the locket, which was wrapped in green paper and tied with a cluster of ostentatious blue ribbons.

8\. "The necklace was a relic from the shrine of a saint. In every charm, a white veronica and the most intricately engraved psalm."

9\. A little known version of the film, in which the heroine enters a convent. After renouncing all ties with the beloved, she was plagued with visions of fire. Smoke shattering the neat rows of stained glass windows.

10\. Her house contained the most elaborate memorial. His cufflinks tarnishing on a white satin pillow.

11\. The wilted corsage. Every shrine burned to the ground.

\*

A History of the Jewelry Box: Glossary of Terms

By Kristina Marie Darling

 

bird. As in the shape of a charm, which was garnished with tiny lacquer roses. When it collided with her watch, their house would murmur with the most startling music.

charm. An item most often used to evoke memories. Consider the piercing green eyes of the pewter bird that he gave to her on her name day. Its little rhinestones blazing against her black wool coat.

clasp. The broken lobster hook heralded his loss of interest in her formidable collection of jewelry. Despite the infinite variety of her pins and brooches, his trinkets no longer appeared beneath her window.

dancer. A tiny porcelain figure that collapsed beneath the lid of an elaborately engraved box. After his departure, she sorted rhinestones as it twirled on a white pedestal.

field. Meaning the green expanse outside her window, which was overrun with dead poppies. They realized that the landscape, rather than affection for one another, was the source of their inexplicable euphoria.

locket. Characterized by a hidden compartment, most often containing photographs of the beloved. Upon opening the glittering charm, she realized that its frame had always been empty.

forgive the messiness of this response - pressed for time.

please ask for clarification if there are specific points that might be helpful.

so. on to the poem.

i feel like there are competing impulses in the poem. on the one hand, the poem wants to move beyond metaphor and into a surreal realm where sunlight is an ingredient in the soup.

on the other, it wants to cling to metaphor as a poetic device, rather than a facet of a strange reality: “I set the table with plates as if they were stones” - i wanted to see it cut loose fully into the realm of the surreal.

\*

in the list, "purple" isn't a description of Romaine, but a member of the list that stands parallel to the other concrete items. so we have this movement of turning abstract things into concrete ingredients (sunlight, purple, etc.) - this is by far one of the most interesting strategies of the poem

\*

a stew filled with basil and sun (something needs to happen here with “sun” – I most enjoyed reading this line as being about an actual “sun” in the soup: what about “filled with basil and a molten star (or sun)”?

\*

“no one arrives” perfect. could we seal the deal by linking it to the narrator doing some action that continues to… serve guests?

No one arrives.

I take their coats and…

\*

a series of metaphors that almost, but don’t quite, let themselves be connected as “real,” metaphors with some particular “image” value –

bangle skins

a vase of curls (I love the way in which this can be read as “a vase filled with curls” or… a vase constructed of curls.)

\*

I set the table with stones

“as though they were stones” this line, for me, is emblematic of the poem’s… gravity, the way it sometimes recoils from its own surrealism

\*

“small things can be cut / and tossed into a bowl”

the depersonalized violence of that line is beautiful (I mean, of course, in terms of how it contributes to the poem)

\*

blood oranges the shape of mother’s womb (again - why not make the leap all the way into the surreal? the blood oranges aren't a metaphor for mother's womb, but, dream-like, they ARE mother's womb)

\*

the surreal disconnection of the narrator’s emotions from the surrounding environment and actions fits quite well the dream-like or traumatized metaphors of the poem: there’s been some “cut” that the narrator hasn’t been able to experience yet.

might want to emphasize the traumatic repetition compulsion quality of the “cutting” and preparing food, etc.

\*

Romaine, purple,

opened to olive oil.  A stew

filled with basil

\[\]and \[a molten\] sun\[.\]

I set the table with ~~plates~~

~~as though they are~~ stones.

For the centerpiece, cherry blossoms

in a vase of curls. Small things can be cut

and tossed into a bowl, the blood

oranges remind me of mother's womb. \[probably too crude, but I thought “womb” was far too impersonal. “Blood oranges arranged like mother’s / count”

No one arrives. i take

their coats, carve

bangle skins from apples.

~~grab the salt shaker. ?~~

\[\]

On the terrace, the matryoshka doll

from childhood remains broken.

Her wounds are like bread

split and laid out after rising.

\[I start again\]

even though the image of the matryoshka doll as a figure for psychological interiority is old, you make it new, here. it works because you turn it against itself with the same surreal image tactics that work in the rest of the poem: the matryoshka doll doesn’t “split open” into a successive series of self-contained interiors – no, the “wound” is something that cuts through all those layers, melds them together “like bread / split and laid out after rising.”

to my mind, this is the central image of the poem, or the image that most fittingly summarizes the rest

(also - you have the elements of a list poem here:

1.   Romaine, purple, opened to olive oil

2.   A stew filled with basil and sun

3.   the table, set with stones

4.   cherry blossoms in a vase of curls

5.   small things cut and tossed in a bowl

6.   blood oranges shaped like wombs

she's talked about as an experimental poet, but my sense is that she also achieves a pretty consistent lyricism and investment in verse as a stage for the personal:

Eyes

BY RAE ARMANTROUT

After John Milton

Our light is never spent.

Is spent.

Thus have we scooped out

maceration reservoirs.

We will blaze forth 

what remains

as pixels.

Great angels 

ﬂy at our behest

between towers,

along axons and dendrites,

so that things stand

as they stand

in the recruited present.

Source: Poetry (June 2009).

**[Patchin PL Speakeasy](http://www.tinroofalleypoets.org/poetry_boards/index.php/board,144.0.html) / [Re: Creating The Dialog Between Poet and Critic](http://www.tinroofalleypoets.org/poetry_boards/index.php/topic,16988.msg125998.html#msg125998)**

« **on:** May 15, 2012, 12:22 PM »

i see we're talking about a very particular kind of criticism here. might help to think about various kinds / categories / capacities sometimes called "criticism"

**1. evaluative criticism:** the kind of thing that happens in the NYT Book Review. It's an aesthetic judgment of a text that measures its value according to some particular scale. this kind of criticism belongs to developed works of developed voices, and can function as a sort of filter for the decent and not-so-decent. the danger in these forums is to make aesthetic judgments from the perspective of particular styles / schools and apply them to unfinished works-in-progress and developing voices.

so an example of the kind of critical malpractice would be taking a poem in progress, and because that particular poem in progress is not working, damning the style / school / aesthetic it's trying to achieve or work within. so for example: if my sense is that a series of dense or opaque metaphors are not working in a particular piece, a misapplication of evaluative criticism would be to go on to argue against dense or opaque metaphors as a stylistic device.

it's putting the cart before the horse.

**2. interpretive criticism:** this tends to belong to the finished work too, rather than the work-in-progress --- although it can usually be productively combined with workshop-type criticism to help the author see things he or she might not have otherwise seen in how their poem is working and what it might ultimately be. it's not a judgment of the piece being critted but a detailed explication of how it works, as it is and on its own terms.

i speak from five years of experience teaching the analytical and interpretive study of literature as a graduate student instructor at u of m, when i say that this capacity, to me, although related to the ability to write poetry, is pretty radically distinct. and that it's the capacity that the finished poem most benefits from - there's a symbiotic sort of relationship that can develop between poetry and interpretive criticism.

**3. workshop criticism:** this is the kind of thing that is most helpful in a setting like this. again, i'm speaking from many years of academic creative writing workshop experience, in a variety of roles from participant, to submitter, to workshop moderator.  this capacity, like interpretive criticism, approaches the critted text on its own terms, what it's trying to achieve or accomplish and how it can best do that.

this is the most detailed of the critical capacities, and ideally it can do a line-by-line evaluation of the critted piece as measured against its own internal goals and desires, sort of against the poem's own immanent ideal. it's also the capacity that is most closely related to the capacity for and knowledge of the craft of poetry.

**4. poetics:** not really criticism as such, but the critical explication of poetic method or style or school, written by poets themselves. this often takes the form of a manifesto or polemic. 

the selection from breton's manifesto for surrealism, posted in experimental verse, is an example of this genre.

in fact, i think it would be useful to have a place to post example statements of poetics. or to craft our own (not that i'm feeling up to that, at the moment, but just as an option.

\*

in terms of the dialogue between poet and critic on a forum like this, in terms specifically of workshop type criticism, it's hard to say.

on the one hand, the poet's explication of what she's doing in response to the critter can often function as an excuse or screen to shield the poet from receiving valid criticism.

on the other hand, critters are very rarely perfectly objective, and so there's often room for the poet to push back just a bit against the critter's suggestions. this can also be a really great way for the poet to practice skills like interpretive criticism, in defending her own choices, or poetics, in articulating / defending her own poetic stylistics.

i guess a balance of both would be ideal. i often find myself wanting to push back against crits perhaps more than i should - particularly crits that respond from a general, broad, or vague position,

but then also after that initial impulse still taking in, reflecting on, and attempting to learn from whatever criticism it was, even if that criticism was perhaps over-broad.

just my thoughts,

matt

i just took "I" and bolded the abstractions - just to highlight to what degree you're relying on them

    I

To look with **error ridden** tired-night eyes,

**Stress not forgiveness given, stress that we**

**Forget. Mind not such a goal, but disguise.**

**Behold reason’s reunion, presence be**

**In** plain mind-sight, **to offer surface end,**

**Allow it full potential so you see.**

The gap that one always air-like transcends

Erects a gateless fence made of concrete.

Flight restricted, halted **such message-send.**

Follow me, scale the path of those **elite.**

**Eternally driven, but always near.**

**Abandon transport, now parade on feet.**

 

i am not an enormous fan of robert frost. nonetheless, he does know his craft, and this is a very famous modern terza rima with which i'm sure you are familiar:

I have been one acquainted with the night. (a)

I have walked out in rain—and back in rain. (b)

I have outwalked the furthest city light. (a)

I have looked down the saddest city lane. (b)

I have passed by the watchman on his beat (c)

And dropped my eyes, unwilling to explain. (b)

I have stood still and stopped the sound of feet (c)

When far away an interrupted cry (d)

Came over houses from another street, (c)

But not to call me back or say good-bye; (d)

And further still at an unearthly height (a)

One luminary clock against the sky (d)

Proclaimed the time was neither wrong nor right. (a)

I have been one acquainted with the night. (a)

i just want to point out the relatively diminutive presence of abstractions, in the poem, its reliance on concrete details. the poem deals with such profound themes that its sort of easy to miss that it never breaches the concrete narrative context of a late night walk.

and your syntax here is a little bit tortured - i have nothing against non-standard anything, or breaking grammatical rules, or any other kinds of rules, or even with not making sense.

the problem is that the distortions here seem to spring from an attempt to strike a... a sort of voice of humanist wisdom a la the philosophical fortune cookie.

let me put that in a different way:

the distortions in clarity and sense seem to stem more from a heroic effort to meet a form that is too much for the poem, rather than as something your poem is actually trying to achieve.

i think it might be helpful to ask yourself and spend a little time thinking about:

*Why* am I writing in terza rima? what does this particular form add to the poem? what does it mean to write in terza rima today, as opposed to 14th century florence?

what famous terza rima poems is mine in conversation with? why? how does it use the terza rima differently?

i hesitate to suggest that you abandon the form, or suggest that you turn the poem into something other than what you wanted it to be.

but... this is a very ambitious form, and it seems to me, that with the degree of editing that needs to be done, addressing all those issues and still maintaining the metrical and rhyme pattern is basically an impossible task.

at the very very least, i'd suggest chopping it down to one terza rima, so that there's less to juggle while you're revising.

\*

that said, don't get the wrong idea here. there was some really interesting language in this piece, much of which has already been pointed out to you.

"tired-night eyes" and many others

but at the moment these seem to be buried in abstractions to such a degree that it's very difficult to focus on them.

**[Patchin PL Speakeasy](http://www.tinroofalleypoets.org/poetry_boards/index.php/board,144.0.html) / [Re: Creating The Dialog Between Poet and Critic](http://www.tinroofalleypoets.org/poetry_boards/index.php/topic,16988.msg126011.html#msg126011)**

« **on:** May 15, 2012, 12:55 PM »

i'd also like to say something about my sense of the critter's source of authority.

i've found it most effective both in how i myself think about workshop criticism, and in how i "sell" workshop participation and encourage others to participate, to think of the real core of this capacity as simply my own subjective reaction to the piece.

that is, everyone has the authority to offer workshop criticism - even you, nemesis - because the authority to offer this criticism is not a particular body of knowledge, either of a literary tradition or of the nuts and bolts of poetic craft, but your own personal reaction to the piece.

the trick lies in paying attention to yourself when you're reading the poem. you are, whether you'd like to or not, always already producing a kind of internal self-dialogue about the poem you're reading that can come in the form of simply how you're processing the piece.

do you like it or not? did you get this or that sense from it?

and then the real "skill" that's involved in workshop critting is in tracking down in as much detail as possible the chain of events that moved between your reading of the poem and your reaction to it; and articulating this relationship between poem and your subjective reaction in as much detail as possible.

so you've identified that you like this part but not that part, or that you were confused at this part but not at that, or that you though the poem meant this or that....

cool. now track it down. at exactly which line did you begin to have this sense? what particular words triggered it, and how? etc.

the more you're willing to track down and articulate that process in detail, the more helpful and detailed your crits will be.

but that's just my own limited perspective and what i've found works in encouraging students to start workshopping

(a similar principle works for me in teaching interpretive criticism...)

My concern and my appeal to the staff here are basically selfish. I’d like more responses to my poems, more responses to my responses to your poems, and in general much more active dialogue and conversation. And the way I’ve been seeking that is to invest plenty of energy in your poems. My selfish concern isn’t really directed at the staff at all, I just don’t know who else I could direct it at, who else I might be able to get any purchase in persuading him or her to participate more.

I assume, Kay, that the “going off the spool” and arrogance things are obliquely directed at me, not because of undue paranoia (although there’s plenty of that), but because no one (barring champagne shoes and Skadee) has responded to my posts on the AX in over two weeks, ever since I picked a fight with Bill. And because Bill has explicitly expressed similar sentiments.

Actually, Kay, I doubt that was directed at me—there's that paranoia again—but I know that others feel that way.

My investment here is being misunderstood. I’m not posting “because \[I.\] think \[my\] poem is the greatest thing on the face of the earth and \[I am\] really posting to teach \[you\].” I don’t understand how anyone can see it in that way. I’ve completely revised and even scrapped poems in response to your feedback. I’ve been very consistent in my responsiveness to detailed feedback. How can you think I’m posting out of arrogance?

Look, I get it – I can be pretty abrasive.

At the same time, arguing with you is my strange way of generating sincere dialogue.

My appeal to the staff, although selfish in nature, is also very practical in terms of the health of the site.

April saw more new topics than the site has seen since October 2008, and more new posts than it’s seen since September 2008. May is poised to see as many or more.

Between April and May—with May not finished yet—the site has seen as many new posts as 2011 combined.

As far as I can tell, the beginning of 2012 saw the site on the verge of extinction, with only 8 new topics for the entire month of January.

Regardless of how you feel about my abrasiveness, I’ve been putting a lot of energy into the site and the poems people post here, because I care about poetry and I don’t currently have a place to express that care. I’m putting a lot of energy in because I’d like some dialogue and conversation about poetry—your poem, my poem, his poem, her poem.

But that energy is not coming back in my direction. And I’m starting to feel just a touch ridiculous.

have you thought of sending it to her directly?

couldn't hurt to try.

i'm really not sure what i think about voice and page. post-structuralist academic dogma (at least here at u of m) is that the idea of "voice" is an illusion generated by various kinds of poetic devices on the page. (don't ever let anyone tell you that the academy's mission is "freedom of inquiry")

in other words, you're going to get disparaging looks if you ever talk about "voice" without the quotation marks.

on the other hand, i almost always queue my poems to voice - that is, in my personal writing, i do tend to write as a script -- i even "hear" punctuation, what a dash should sound like, what two line breaks rather than one should sound like, etc.

and yet my experience is that the way i'm hearing a poem scripted in my head is much, much different than what another reader imagines.

yes - we could get some interesting exercises going here.

like, take a poem - maybe something difficult to read, like a concrete poem - and have one poet create an mp3.

and then, without the second poet seeing the original text on a page, have the next person turn the mp3 back into a script.

is that clear?

or we could do lots of variations of something along those lines.

\*

as to readings on the internet, the most extreme example i can think of is steve mccaffery's "carnival."

the "text" to the "poem" is posted here in experimental, as well as a video of steve performing it.

it might be worthwhile to take a look at the crazy, schizophrenic images of the text and compare them with his reading.

just for kicks.

so now that i've put my foot in my mouth (tastes like socks, by the way), let me retrace my steps a little bit.

a handful of suggestions / ideas w respect to board format and participation - take them or leave them:

1.   do more to encourage reciprocity on the ax:

a.   post a set of AX posting “suggestions,” in a visible place, such as at the top of the list, including the suggestion to offer feedback on at least two poems for each one you post.

b.   somewhere, maybe in a link in this top-posted note, offer examples of what a critique can look like. not a model for what a critique has to be, but a couple of examples of how to jump into the process for those who might not be sure what they have to offer or how to offer it.

c.   mention it to people personally every now and then. just as a suggestion.

2.   ask users to participate in composing a series of poems about how awesome TRAP is. then post them in the critique section of other active (or inactive) poetry boards.

3.   I still think a forum all by it’s lonesome to practice and post traditional forms, like the sonnet etc., would be a great idea.

4.   so we’ve mentioned instances where a critical debate between poet and critter gets started in a way that leaves the poem lonesome. I think that could be very productive if we could focus it in some way – start a place for “critical debates” and move or copy posts there when a critical debate gets started.

5.   go out of our way to message new members. I’ve noticed a couple of people register without posting – maybe a PM to that kind of person encouraging them to jump in

6.   I don’t understand where the broader dialogue about the history and craft of poetry is. again – possibility of a place to post famous poems and discuss them. I started the “interesting poems” post in patchin pl speakeasy for this purpose. just out of personal curiosity – what are your influences? anyone willing to post a favorite poem or two?

sure, it comes down to personal taste.

at the same time, i've always thought that a major way to measure growth is in terms of ability to gauge how the poem will go out into the world, and shape it accordingly --

or really, for me it's much more general than that - it's how one mind makes sense of another, and communication -- jumping across that mutual unintelligibility -- is ridiculously difficult -- for me, that kind of capacity is pretty synonymous with mastery (like, in the sense of mastering a skill or capacity, or even in the sense of a mastering a spiritual discipline, rather than the master-slave sense)

and the only way i can learn about the effects of what happens when i send something out, what kinds of transformations it goes through on its way from my head to yours, is when it's reflected back at me.

so thanks.

-matt

Hi Elise,

You're setting up a poignant and reflective poem, here. Just some brainstorming below.

\*

line break suggestions are a plus - also, a couple of ideas:

I'm wondering how it would read without "Remember how" and "We ate"? These verbs are both implied by the rest.

I thought stanza three needs revision - I'd rather you communicated "two kids / two parents / laughing" with more specific details, as in the first two stanzas - as part of the narrative rather than an intrusion of the narrator...  Example: "Elise's shiny new cowboy boots..." or "Mom burnt her fingers on the goat from the..."

I agree with witt's suggestion to cut the final line.

I see where you're going with the final stanza, and I think it could be powerful, but I was thrown off just a bit by the metaphor you choose. "Patched up" seems to come out of nowhere. We get shiny (new) stuff, like the cowboy boots, and the shiny day.

Isn't the memory of the "shiny day" supposed to be like the "patch," covering up the not-quite-so-shiny reality?

There is a strong parallel in the poem's ideas, between the day/memory and the "patch," that is dampened because the parts of the metaphor mismatch. I was looking for either... a "something-that-makes-things-that-aren't-shiny-look-shiny" family --- or some "things-that-look-patched-up-but-are-actually-ripped" events or things in the first couple of stanzas in place of the "shiny" things we find there.

That was far from clear, but I hope you see what I mean.

-Matt

**[Fourth Factory Poetry Workshop](http://www.tinroofalleypoets.org/poetry_boards/index.php/board,147.0.html) / [poetry v. philosophy](http://www.tinroofalleypoets.org/poetry_boards/index.php/topic,17063.msg126813.html#msg126813)**

« **on:** June 08, 2012, 11:55 PM »

\*Philosophy - in the broadest sense of thinking rigorously / systematically

...all they want to do

is tie the poem to a chair with rope

and torture a confession out of it.

They begin beating it with a hose

to find out what it really means.

                  --Billy Collins

What's the relationship between thinking critically and writing poetry? I can't think of a single philosopher who was a great poet, or of a poet who was a great philosopher. But this is an old debate -- Plato kicked the poets out of the ideal city.

Myself, I go between - I have a job that requires me to think critically and articulate that in writing. My first love is poetry, but I find I can't really embrace both at the same time: I was on a creative roll for awhile, not really pushing forward on the critical work... now I've gotten into the critical work, and I couldn't write a poem to save my soul.

So... any thoughts? does poetry work against critical thinking? help it along? When Billy Collins (no, I don't like Billy Collins, but whatever) talks about "tortur\[ing\] a confession out of" the poem "to find out what it really means," do we go along with this antagonism? Does critical thinking takes a violent, demystifying stance towards poetry?

What does poetry do that thought can't? Thought that poetry can't?

Does the capacity / practice of rigorous and systematic thinking squash out the poetic brain? If so, how or why?

In what ways is poetry itself a mode of thought, and how does that mode differ from the other?

just rambling here. if you can latch on to any of those, or branch off in some other direction, cool.

Let me reframe my initial response as a claim that might be able to frame a conversation:

I've seen several people on the AX (this is for you too, Bill) take aggressive stances against "obscurity" by blaming it on academia.

My claim is that the tyranny of clarity, "common rules of prose," and emotional transparency is far more representative of institutionalized academic poetry and its legions than of any anti-academic or lowbrow position.

The example I give in response to Steve is the wholesale alliance between IBPC judges and academia. Marjorie Perliff's article, linked in the topic "on poetry stagflation" in Patching PL Speakeasy, is also highly relevant..

My specific criticism of "academia bashing," when used to bolster an aggressive stance against "obscurity," is that it is completely disingenuous -- it's a political move that presents itself as a somehow ostracized or censured margin, while actually relying on the authority and influence of the mainstream position that has been in part enforced by academia.

\*\*\*

What's with the academia bashing?

I challenge you to find more than a handful of past IBPC judges who don't work in or have some strong professional connection to academia.

Respect where respect is due.

skaadee -

this poem has some great descriptions that crystallize a strong persona

and the way it creates images of the past, and sets them against the present, generates some leverage that's difficult to resist -

even if we're not drawn to the particular values or sentiments the poem's past represents, we can't help but acknowledge them:

so many perfect juxtapositions. my favorites were S4 (whiskey), S12 (the president), S15 (porn), and S18 (horse sense)-- also the billionaires who aren't oil tycoons stanza, although i'm wondering if it should be grouped together with S18?

now for suggestions:

the short:

\*it felt earlier than the 40s, to me (apart from the "war effort").

\*it needs some serious trimming. weigh the most powerful stanzas, be brutal about which ones are absolutely necessary, and which are variations that repeat a theme you've expressed more powerfully elsewhere. it will still be a powerful poem without the cuts. but my sense is that it needs them to be fully developed. if you're interested, just let me know and i can reflect my sense of where cuts could happen.

\*also i saw some repetition at the line level. just an example: a bar named after an owner named

\*the N-word stanza: here's why it falls flat: it's a moment when our old spice, unfiltered camels protagonist shrinks back and makes obeisance to the 21st century. the character you're creating does not use phrases like "the N-word." see what i mean? my sense it to either bite the bullet, and let the character use the word, or cut it. if it were me, i'd cut, because most people won't read it as a character in a poem but attribute it to you personally.

\*one last thing: i don't have firm ideas, but i'm wondering if you've had different thoughts about organization, in the course of drafting the poem? i wanted the descriptive, narrative stanzas (S2-3 and S8) to be set off more distinctly from the "I want..." stanzas. i was wondering how it would read if S2-3 started the poem?

Dear cipra,

I have decided, on the basis of your poem, to alter the objective criteria of what makes “a poem.” From now on, a given piece of writing may only be defined as “poem” if it exhibits the following qualities:

a single, eleven line stanza

with two distinct, alternating linear forms

of which the first consists of five alliterative verbs

(with the exception of the penultimate line, which shall consist of two verbs, an adjective, noun, and verb, in that order)

and the second of an impersonal command,

depicting violent or graphic imagery

and having the stress pattern – x – x – x --  (no substitutions possible.)

and the rhyme scheme below:

A

A

B

A

C

D

A

D

E

F

A

All writings purporting to be "poems," but not exhibiting the above-mentioned qualities, shall henceforth be defined as "drivel."

On the basis of my authoritative redefinition, it’s possible that the above is the world’s only poem.

rg and kay -

you are both right in claiming that in most social contexts, including this current online forum, satire as a form of dialogue will not work. and that if it's resulting in hurt feelings, something has broken down in the process.

but i'm having a hard time thinking of an influential cultural movement in which satire wasn't an important form of dialogue.

so let's grant something like, "under most conditions, satire either can't be practiced in a way that's socially productive, or interpreted in a way that's socially productive."

granting that, i guess my question isn't, "why can't we make fun of each other here, in these conditions, where satire will be practiced and interpreted as destructive?" but rather, "what are the conditions that make it possible to practice and interpret satire as a form of productive dialogue?"

take this poem below:

**Quote**

At least we both know how shitty the world is. You \[Ginsberg\] wearing a

      beard as a mask to disguise it. I wearing my tired smile. I

      don’t see how you do it. One hundred thousand university

      students marching with you. Toward

A necessity which is not love but is a name.

King of the May. A title not chosen for dancing. The police

Civil but obstinate. If they’d attacked

The kind of love (not sex but love), you gave the one hundred

   thousand students I’d have been very glad. And loved the

   policemen. Why

Fight the combine of your heart and my heart or anybody’s

   heart. People are starving.

                        \[Jack Spicer’s final poem\]

the poem is a more open form of critique than satire, but the principle is the same. the poem criticizes ginsberg, his poems, and in general the poetics of public identity ("bearded image") that ginsberg constructs through his poems.

if the conditions weren't in place to make this productive, then ginsberg would get hurt feelings and either shut down or take it to him personally. but the poem isn't personal--it's a dialogue that addresses ginsbeg's poetics. ginsberg can respond by defending and elaborating his own position, or by modifying it a little bit, acknowledging the critique.

i don't feel like i'm making my point very clear. but the main thing is that i do see conditions elsewhere in history or culture that make productive satire possible, that turn it into a back-and-forth. what could make it so elsewhere?

1\) Satire, though barbed, is a form of personal regard--

--Name a movement or period in poetry—any movement or period—and you’ll find poems in which poets make fun of each other, their verse, philosophies of poetry, and opposing camps. Matt,

i don't know enough about your style or history to say for sure, but to my mind, you have in just a short time made some pretty big leaps towards economy of language, precision, and crispness (all qualities that i often lack).

not that you've arrived, but i wanted to reflect for you that I've noticed changes in the way you write.

\*

small points first: i think the context gives us plenty of information to understand that moor is the boat kind, rather than the Arab or Berber conquerors of spain kind. (although reading it that way could make for an interesting poem, yes?)

\*the only thing "unattended to" needs to be correct grammar is this: i leak, unattended, ...   unattended as an adjective doesn't need an indirect subject.

\*i love the pun @ berth / birth

Bigger picture stuff:

i think using the boat to talk about desire is a great exercise in concretion and avoiding empty abstraction. i felt that the last two lines were the weakest, and that the poem would resonate more strongly if they were cut.

here's what i saw as the poem's central elements:

I'm on a moor, revving,

my motor dies at berth

shredded fish

sucked into the propeller

\*even though it's clear what's happening, i was wondering if you should separate the whole fish from shredded ones, or make explicit that they're not shredded until they've been sucked in.

\*also, i felt "my motor dies at berth" was the most important line in terms of linking the poems title "desire" with its images. we get the clearest analogy between desire and the boat in that line, and i was actually wondering if there was a way to single it out more, maybe by making it the final line?

\*also, i was wondering if you could use line breaks to signal the motor's death, from faster-paced, longer lines, to syncopated, short, sort of stuttering lines when the motor dies?

I'm on a moor, revving.

The propeller sucks in

fish and shreds them-

my motor

dies

at berth.

-matt

we might be getting somewhere.

i think you're right to distinguish "poetic response" as a broader category, and satire as just one kind of poetic response.

so, that helps me rethink my original question, as something like, "what is it that distinguishes between satire as a poetic response (which can be productive) and satire as petty vindictiveness (which isn't)?"

the beatles example is a good one. what makes it poetic response, rather than (or, at least, in addition to) vindictiveness?

the thing i was trying to say earlier is that i think "direct address" is an important part of poetic response,

and in the examples you're using, the public nature of the direct address is important. the direct response is for the other person, but also for an audience -- two artists responding to each other through an audience.

so far, if we're in agreement, we can say that poetic response is:

-some form of creative work (visual, poetic, etc.)

-a direct address (responding to a specific poet, poem, or... something specific)

-and public (it's for an audience as much as for the other person)

so would we be willing to allow satire or "making fun" the possibility of being constructive, rather than personally vindictive, if it's a creative work, a direct address, and public?

or how should we modify it or add to it to make it work?

(p.s. - i wasn't calling out marxistglue, i was just addressing him directly by starting a game i thought he would be interested in (since it's based on his name, after all) -- i just brought it into the conversation as an example of direct address, not an example of satire, making fun, or teasing)

i'm curious about how disagreements become productive, engines for generating poems and developing poetic style.

i don't want to satirize anything in particular, certainly not your poems.

but here's an example in which i (unsuccessfully) attempted to respond to mojave:

<http://www.tinroofalleypoets.org/poetry_boards/index.php/topic,16872.0.html>

from the title, "objective images," "devoid of sentiment," and "purple \[writing\]" are each quotations or paraphrases of claims mojave made about poetry.

so i took those (as universal claims) to their most absurd conclusions, of which the poem's style is supposed to be an example.

not mean or pointed. not even denying that mojave was right.

but responding to a series of claims in a way that (attempted but failed to) throw them back into his corner, either to clarify and develop further, or modify slightly, or develop into a counter-critique.

back-and-forth.

steve - no poetry sheriff, no posse.

so let's grant, for the sake of argument, that something like rg's standards of conduct above create the space for dialogue, whether critical, poetic, or whatever. dialogue and mutual influence happen within that space.

exercising some kind of external authority--and here i'm still thinking in more general terms, theorizing about how public discourse works in general--would step outside of that space of dialogue. it would be self-defeating.

but i'm thinking about ways that the system of dialogue protects itself, the ways it can regulate its own boundaries from within, as a form of dialogue rather than an exercise of force (i know, this is so absurdly abstruse--forgive me. maybe seraph will chime in to put it into english in fewer than 9000 words)

as an example, SNL, particularly around election time. even though the influence of politicians goes beyond the space of public dialogue, they need the validation of public dialogue to maintain that influence. and SNL, as satire, helps set some limits to that influence, and reminds everyone that the politicians are subject to the standards of community dialogue, too.

at the same time, it offers the politicians a way to respond, to step back into public dialogue by appearing on the show, laughing at themselves, whatever: a way for the politicians to perform their acceptance of public dialogue and its boundaries.

so i'm seeing satire here as both a way of firming up the boundaries of public dialogue - checking attempts to move beyond it into the realm of force or raw power - and at the same time as a legitimate form of dialogue that allows the politician to respond - as long as they do so as a form of public dialogue, according to its standards.

so no sheriff, no posse. i'm just interested in the ways that satire can be productive, necessary. what need does it fulfill, what's its role in maintaining the standards of community dialogue, etc.

and in what ways does the space of community dialogue protect itself, maintain its boundaries.

could satire be one of those ways?

-matt

p.s. i know that much of the above was rambling, obtuse. if it's unclear, just read it like a poem =)

Rg-

In the post quoted below, you outline a set of standards that make community of mutual benefit possible.

These are the standards (mutual respect, constructive criticism, goodwill) that create a space for dialogue.

So that's to say, I'm in complete agreement with the standards of a critical / poetic community--or for any community of public discourse--that you outline above.

EXCEPT FOR:

the kind of circumstance which seraph was pointing out: when a member of a community appears to be taking advantage of its standards by using the space they create for dialogue in order to beef up his or her own authority, influence, or whatever. In other words, when it appears that a critter is only interested in trashing poems, and not at all in the poem or poet itself and the ways it might be possible for them to improve.

Goodwill. So the (unspoken) question seraph responds to is, "How do you police or enforce those standards of community? What forms of dialogue exist that can reinforce those boundaries without brute force, without stepping outside of the space for dialogue?" (satire?)

With the "insensitivity" thing, I was just suggesting that, if a member of the community appears to be sincerely trying to work within those standards, his or her missteps or offenses are part of the process. Nothing to worry about. For example, in this community, if a critter comes down hard on a poem--maybe even too hard, or harder than necessary--but it appears that his or her intent was to help the poem and poet, and that his or her motivation was to assist the poem and help it grow, then the critter's harshness is in agreement with your standards of community. 

(oh seraph - yours was definitely more succinct. i need you as a wingman.)

[**Quote from: cafeRg on June 20, 2012, 06:02 PM**](http://www.tinroofalleypoets.org/poetry_boards/index.php/topic,17091.msg127078.html#msg127078)

Hi Steve ..no. I was just practicing my Don Rickles ..we're cool

---------------

Critics come in many different flavors and styles, as does poets. When we write a poem we are the poet. When we critique a poem we become a teacher or mentor. The poem you are critiquing should tell you the level of the poet you're dealing with. So you should be flexible enough to mentor from that level, as a starting point. Don't wanna help the neophyte? Then don't take on the role of that poets mentor. We should be encouraging and motivating. Not act like know-it-all bullies, we don't have time for your dumbass writing.

A good poet is happy to share their tips and techniques. Let's say you're an expert poet and you want some help with a new poem. The critic comes in, they're an expert to, and tells you your work is a piece of garbage. How would that make you feel? It doesn't matter if you're an expert or a newbie, both deserve respect, some useful direction and encouragement.

The old adage: the student is only as good as the teacher. How's your students doing?

steve - i have to respectfully but strongly disagree. you don't correct a toddler in the same way you correct a teenager. not all--but most--neophytes are relatively flexible and receptive to feedback. they require very little force to start making adjustments and moving their practice in different directions. come down like a bomb on that kind of person, and you're often shutting down the very motivation that could have driven them to improve. use the amount of force that's necessary, no more.

whereas those who are established often become quite sure of themselves, and will only budge in response to greater force. such as mockery.

yes, both the weak and the strong need a kick in the ass, sometimes. but again, the amount of force that will be experienced as "a kick in the ass" varies from person to person, and should be adjusted accordingly.

-matt

p\. s.: i'd also suggest this as another quality of constructive satire:

it has the potential to be productive when and only when less pointed forms of address will not or have not worked.

rg - i did construct the outline of an implied narrative. that's as much as i can gather, and several of those are assumptions. the kind of alien isn't specified - all i know is that it's an entity, probably non-human, that if i'm taking that line literally can move through space without a spaceship, perhaps by skimming across the surface of outer space quickly enough and with wide enough feet that it doesn't sink, even while carrying a sword. and that the particular entity is a hero / fabulous messiah alien - singled out from the rest of his/her kind.

as to the line "before and after god what comes"

would you like me to go into its possible meanings?

it could mean -

\* o god, what is it that will come before and after the white star implosion?

\* Q: what is coming? A: the god of before and after

\* displaced voice of narrator: the before and after god      the protagonist: what comes?

\* what comes before god and after god?

\*the entity races through space in an indefinite zone that is outside of (before and after) the laws of the physical universe (god), and the effect of his incomprehensible space travel is such that it causes other kinds of entities or the universe itself to ask, "what is coming?"

\*what are the effects on a planet in the time leading up to and the time following a cataclysmic cosmic event, such as the birth of a black hole? what does the race of entities go through, knowing that the end of their civilization is coming, and there's nothing they can do about it? and what is left of the civilization in the smoking aftermath?

\*the cataclysmic forces of the universe itself (like the white dwarf implosion) are a sort of "before and after god," in that they, even in their destructiveness, "assimilate what has been" and "make new and fresh," -- and it is this implacable force of unfeeling but necessary cosmic renewal that is coming.

\*etc.

so. now i have answered your question at length, i might be able to offer some constructive feedback if you could orient me towards what you would like the poem to ultimately be/do.

or not.

Great question(s). It seems to me contemporary poetry is very much a culture of writing, as opposed to a culture of reading. On the one hand, despite cries that the sky is falling and that no one is interested in poetry anymore, poetry today enjoys a much wider practice, readership, and potential for educational and financial opportunities (in the form of stipends for grad students, teaching positions, government funding for the arts, and so on) than at any other time in history. On the other hand, this increased readership / consumer-base for poetry is composed almost entirely of poets. It's just that there are far more poets writing than ever before.

\*

ok but that didn't really address your question: basically, i don't read poetry for pleasure or entertainment, at least not in the same way i read a novel or watch a show. I don't sit down and casually flip through a book of poems to go to sleep, for example. When I read poetry, I'm always looking for something. And when I find the thing/poem/language/whatever that I'm looking for, that one thing becomes important--I orbit around it for awhile. So I guess that's to say--reading poetry is definitely not a quantity thing, for me. It's a sorting and sifting, and when I find a poem or a voice or a poet that shines through all the rest, I grab onto it and hold it close, whether that means emulating and incorporating aspects of the style or ideas, or reading and reading and rereading to understand the poem, or in any way I can to make it mine--a part of the way I think and write, and a part of the reason poetry has meaning to me.

Like--I've put at least 30 hours in researching lit mags over the past couple of weeks. Searching, but as a writer--trying to find out what mags publish what, what styles work where, how this person did this or that, and of course looking for poems I like. And off the top of my head, only one poem that I encountered in that entire process really sticks out in my memory:

so what

George McKim

from elimae may/june 2012

\*

smoke that gazes into

yellow as darkness

what should i pray for, my

starved poems? (their

          uniforms

          floating across the secret river)

          but now i'm sick and

          so what if my hands

          are filled with voices

          so what?

\*\*

Now, stylistically and formally, I read poems that were more impressive, more polished. But this is the one that I took away from the entire reading process, the one I latched onto. I'll keep it forever, return to it, share it with other people, write poems that subtly respond to it or incorporate some of its phrasing or sentiment--I will make it mine, because it's beautiful. And then this one poem joins the others I've collected, and each individual poem fits together in strange new ways.

But if I'd read hundreds of poems and found none to make my own, I wouldn't feel like I'd really read any poetry at all.

cankerworm: revision \#4

“years the cankerworm ate: a psalm”

Joel 2: 25:                        ...the years that the locust has eaten, the cankerworm,

and the caterpiller, and the palmerworm, my great army which I sent among you.

Awake, a ghost in the eaves,

fitful bulbs buzzing above--

I breathe. Milky eyes wide

with webs, stomach in knots,

fitful with dread, alone but for

my baby-soft, sad-hair head.

God again, awake in the night,

a ghost in the leaves: I am.

The slow skitter of years

turns to hours in this dark.

That which turns to May

only yesterday was March—

and then beneath these bulbs

September starts—I start

and flutter, I clutch

the strands of strings,

I fumble with the fraying heart.

I have suffered some sad thing

in the silence I keep, named only

by the blankness of an hour killed,

or the distant noise of a leak.

The first gray milk of morning

drips through the shuttered blinds,

carrying a sole, small note:

a dart from the mouth of a morningbird,

defying the bars of night.

             

I will

rise with morning.

I will

shake off the night’s longing.

p\. s. Rg:

I just wanted to acknowledge that the rewrite of the last post was rude. I'm sorry -- I didn't intend it as revision suggestions for your poem, but as what it is: a rewrite / adaptation that's trying to chew on this problem of what kinds of editorial strategies can move a poem between different styles. so please consider my reply @ post \#18 the extent of my revision ideas or critical suggestions, and the rewrite at @post \#21 something else entirely.

i'm still chewing on this idea, how revisions can take a poem in wildly different stylistic directions.

for example, the rewrite was my best stab at moving a poem to the "mainstream" style--

here's my formula:

let all stanzas = symmetrical rectangles

let all stanzas contain roughly the same number of lines

let there be a narrative framework for all content / images that appear in the poem

let narrative proceed in a linear fashion, A--\>B--\>C

let there be no missing or implied steps in the narrative progression

let grammar = strunk and white

\*

(just in case it's not clear, this is all slightly tongue-in-cheek).

\*

so - the question of what kinds of editorial strategies could shift a poem into the experimental is much more difficult, because "experimental" doesn't mean any one thing. so for example, your poem is already "experimental" in its use of visual shape: it partially displaces the creation of meaning from things like linear narrative etc. into the material field of space on a page. i'd go out on a limb and say that you seem to have both a preference and a talent for experimenting with concrete/visual forms.

so, rather than thinking of one kind of editorial formula for "experimental," we'd have to cut that up into a number of different strategies. so, we'll start with concrete, since your poem is already working with that.

oh btw: in the poem's visual shape, i see the right-hand half of a butterfly. see the wings? (perhaps of angelic beings skipping across space?). it would be cool to play around w/ or create a version that mirrors, in the left-hand side, the visual shape of the right hand side--so that you arrive at the complete visual shape of the wings. (in fact, if you go there, i know of a mag that might be interested...)

also, i see the possibility for flipping the poem on its side and seeing it as a wavelength or frequency--

i don't know. so, this second part--what kinds of editorial strategies could transform poems into various experimental styles--this is wide open.

does anyone else want to work on this question? and rg is it ok if your poem is the starting point?

-matt

seraph --

i'm finding myself in agreement with some of Bill's suggestions. He's right about S1, but I don't think rearrangement packs as much punch: consider relieving the editor of her potential ammo by adding commas:

Your hair, spilling

over the white pillow, so silken

it made me blink.    (how would you feel about, "so silken / that I blinked" or "so silken / I had to shut stinging eyes" or "so silken / it stung my eyes" -- something like the latter two examples would tie it more directly to the "piercing beauty" of the final stanza. the silky hair stinging the eyes, or making the narrator close her eyes or avert her stinging eyes or something: this would foreshadow the final stanza and give us a satisfying ring structure.

\*i think your current arrangement of S2 is perfectly justifiable, and that it would lose something by placing "youth's spirit" first (i still feel that "youth" and "spirit" "anxiety" and "adventure" right next to each other is too abstract for one stanza... "youth's anxiety / for the next adventure," "the impatience of the young / for tomorrow" ...? (no, those aren't working so well...)

\*i found myself compelled by Bill's arrangement of S3 and S4. i'm not fundamentally concerned with the grammar, but i felt the stanzas read more powerfully that way. i love the break at "awkward / angle" -- you see why that's compelling? like the line of the hair broken by the awkward angle of her neck, the line of the poem is skewed by the awkward placement of the line, breaking apart adj. and noun. how did it read to you?

although i was not terribly concerned about the hierarchy of cause and effect, i really enjoyed the way S4 read, moving from "lost beauty pierced" to the cold rain: again, we have the poem performing its own theme: the stanza begins with the profound weight and pathos of "lost beauty pierced," and then empties itself out, offering us only cold rain. so the stanza, arranged in that way, actually performs the movement from beauty to lost beauty--also, arranging it that way invests the cold rain with all the energy and meaning of lost beauty: reading "beauty piercing" first, I had a much stronger sense of the bitter rain stinging into their eyes.

« **on:** July 04, 2012, 01:28 PM »

no, this is perfect. my complexity isn't necessarily a virtue--it can be, but it's a liability when i don't know what others perceive as complex or not. i normally have absolutely no idea what comes off as dense or opaque or complex and what as clear--in fact, i've found i absolutely have to have dialogue with other people in order to be clear--this is true in my teaching. i would be very, very terrible at standing up in front of 300 people and giving a prepared lecture--because i would have no cues or interaction for the communication. i need the person who lets me know (normally very politely) that what i just said was completely nonsensical. over-complexity is my flaw, not theirs. but i need interaction to know how to flex whatever the idea is into a shape that can transmit to others. 

(of course, there is a time and place for over-complexity--but i consider it a flaw unless it's intentional, unless i'm aware of what isn't clear, and how.)

so, this poem--i thought was a straightforward, narrative kind of thing--the narrator is in the living room, in the middle of the night ("beneath these (light)bulbs"), all alone, and depressed. time is slipping by incredibly quickly  ("that which turns to may"), and he can't quite grab hold of it, or even name the terror eating away at the edges of reality ("some sad thing.... the blankness of an hour killed")--

and so the poem, in its first part, is painting the scene, and trying to communicate the terrible *absence* of words, the complete *inability* to blame or pin the Terror on anything in particular, or even to call it anything in particular. the Terror i can't name is namelessness itself.

and then the second part (ii. in version one), or the stanza beginning "the first gray milk..." (in the current revision) is the transition from despair to some kind of resolve. the resolve, like the despair, has no distinct name or reason for coming around--it comes in the predawn with the tiny little morning bird singing against the night. so, the sole small note is the... the fragile Word that speaks against the Goliath Namelessness. of course, birdsong is also a figure for the poem--a sole, small note that comes out even in the middle of the night, a little word that bubbles up even in the depths of the nameless Terror--

and the purpose... well, it's just the psalmic movement from despair to resolve/hope.

any of the basic narrative elements (just bare bones, yes) that weren't clear, that's not intentional. and i could benefit very much from your pointing out where it's not clear and how it could become clear.

thanks skaadee,

matt

p.s. i adopted your suggestions @ "silences" and "the night"--also, i was thinking all the way back to "dear Words" the other day, and thinking that you might have been right after all, with "sing." i'm going to try it out.

-

« **on:** July 04, 2012, 01:04 PM »

so rg - i'm going to eat my words and retract my ambitious plan to offer alternative crits--one crit to tend it to the mainstream, one crit to tend it to the experimental.

bravado, i guess. or i'm just realizing i might never sit down to do it.

so--let me tone it down a notch and offer some local feedback on what's here:

\*with the theme of "the two edges of the universe," i thought it would be interesting to make the entities racing to the edge of the universe, to go beyond the edge of matter into the nothingness at the expanding boundary. maybe the universe itself is collapsing and they are racing to its edges to escape, or to find a way out for their people, or whatever.

\*with the whole black hole thing, i think this is actually a strand in theoretical physics:

          the new theory or possibility being that, instead of a universe that compacts down into an infinitely dense point of matter, then explodes outward from the pressure, until the force of that bang dies out, and all the matter falls back to the center again--the cosmos as a giant, eternal back-and-forth accordion, the idea is that black holes actually become the site of new universes:

          not that different from the big bang, except that, in this theory, everything that a black hole sucks up condenses into that infinitely dense point of matter, then explodes in a new big bang. except this big bang takes place *inside* the black hole--the outward force of the explosion isn't enough to escape the gravity well of the hole itself, but it becomes this new universe that expands within it, then contracts and so on.

          and within *that* universe in the black hole, other conglomerations of matter turn into stars and planets, and the white dwarfs implode and create more black holes inside the black hole--and so on.

          so instead of a single, contained event with discrete boundaries--our cosmos--we have this latticework of Russian doll universes.

\*

ok geez sorry about that--that was all to say, i think you could incorporate just a touch more of that sense of grandness / bigness / wonder by making the entities' destination specific: say, they're heading to the edge of the universe, or they're heading into a black hole to find a new universe, or their universe is inside a black hole and they're trying to escape its gravity well. something--not to take away the mystery of the destination / quest, but to anchor that mystery in a particular mystery of physics or whatever.

\*i wanted to see a device besides the simile @ "like ninja swordsmen." you want something that will not compare them to ninja swordsmen, but will make them become ninja swordsmen--all the while making it clear that they are not, in fact, ninja swordsmen.... so something like... "ninja swordsmen of space- / and-time race across the cosmos, / stones that skip on a boiling sea--"

\*and i'm suggesting some rearrangements for the purpose of anchoring narrative: move from S1 directly to --\> S4+5, then back up to the white dwarf star implosion, and so on. this will prepare us to hear the "voice" of the ninja swordsmen right away, and give the narrative context that helps anchor S2-3 --  "ninja swordsmen of space and time....--though a billion voices beg us / to return, we forge on, / to die if we must, or discover / salvation for our species--"

\*and now that the quest narrative is established, then go into the mysteries at the edge of the universe or outside the universe or outside of space-and-time or whatever (now the context for encountering these mysteries has been personalized for your reader, and directly woven into the desperation of our entities)

\*"to find the time / before the beginning, / or the ending that comes / after god--"

\*implosion / explosion / outward---you've got some redundancy here. outward and explosion both communicate the same thing--so stick with one. i think the paradox is much more direct and purposeful with just: "a white dwarf star / imploding outward..."

\*i think the substance / assimilation stanza needs a little massaging, but i will hold off until the next revision.

\*and at the end:  "Arcadia, / we come."

to sum up:    1) make that first stanza hit harder

 

2\) rearrange so that there's a narrative to frame the musings on the mysteries of the universe

3\) do more with the voice of the narrator(s)-- (e.g., "Arcadia, / we come.")--the stoic-doomed warrior voice of our cosmic ninjas is a major pull in the poem--look for ways to emphasize that strength.

-matt

skaadee -- it's an art to describe what's happening in a poem, from a remove. to take the difficult parts of our own almost inarticulable responses to the reading and turn them into prose. you have to stretch the words in strange ways to fit the parts of your reaction that are the most interesting, because they're the most difficult to understand. it felt like you were stretching to catch some of those more difficult aspects of your response to the poem. stretching the literary critical muscles.

high five.

(although, hooking the difficult parts of your response / reading to the particular lines that triggered it can help balance it out. parentheses work for me: in this version, i sense the love between author and word ("sad-hair head")... and so on. just what works for me).

but in any case, thanks for the re-read. i'm still willing to make changes, so throw em my way if you have ideas.

thanks again,

matt

“words no good” as in – I can’t find the words to express it; and as in – I don’t think words will fix the problem.

I appreciate your addressing me directly. it’s frustrating when people will express their concerns only implicitly, or through silence, or refuse outright to acknowledge their existence.

Here’s the thing, Rg—I suppose I could keep on keeping on, but I really don’t want this to be an extension of my professional life. My own poetry is the one area that’s safe from the structured professionalism that demands the rest of my creativity, energy, and time.

In terms of presentation: it’s true that I can have sharp elbows. At the same time, I feel I’ve tried several different approaches, and I’m out of ideas. I’m perfectly willing to receive feedback or reflection, if you have ideas about what’s gone wrong with particular posts, in the past or moving forward, or about how to present them differently. 

just to respond specifically and ask for clarification about your message:

I wasn’t clear about the details of what you’re saying here:

**In your posting you have never said that** (said what? that I’m from academia?)

**If you read what others have said in various post, most don't understand what and why**   (what do “what and why” refer to? I’m not clear as to exactly what it is you’re saying they don’t understand)

**Have you presented yourself correctly? Are the boards only for academia purposes? Or frolic too?** (not clear about what you’re reflecting for me here. have I presented myself as “only for academia purposes”? or no frolic? how so?)

**The best way to teach is to listen to your students but you know that. Are you listening to them?** (I didn’t really want more students, I hoped for peers. that’s how I’ve tried to address people, as equals—i need some reflection as to how it’s misfired. and yes – I’ve clearly missed a vital part of whatever it is they’re telling me)

**Have you also made post that encourage participation?**

I’ve asked for participation in several different ways. I created a psalm exercise and asked others to post their own psalms—no one was willing to participate. I regularly posted poems and asked others to post their favorite poems / poets in Patchin PL Speakeasy—not a single response. for a period of time I was offering relatively detailed feedback for every current poem on the AX – very little response. I’ve posted generic discussion prompts / questions in fourth factory – no response. I set up a personal workshop in which I guarantee detailed feedback – no response. from my perspective, I’ve argued, flattered, fawned, provoked, encouraged, requested, whined, and so on, for participation.

in fact, outside of my first couple of weeks on the site, the only thing I’ve done that HAS generated a substantial response was to complain about the lack of response. that  got everyone involved, sure.

**How many post have you taken the time to praise something about the poem?**

you will not find a single critique in which I haven’t singled out strengths alongside weaknesses. I’m deliberate about lacing critique with praise. if i haven’t offered praise in a way that hits home, or enough praise, i’d appreciate specific examples and suggestions about how I could present praise differently.

**I have mentioned that your post at times are exhaustive,**

yes – I’ve heard this and have attempted to shorten my posts. has that been noticeable, or are still been too long?  excluding, of course, the present, over-wordy response  =)

here’s the short of it:

if I’m going to continue investing energy in the site, I need feedback and reflection about what’s working and not working in the way I’m presenting myself—not just once but semi-regularly as I make adjustments. i’ve presented myself in a number of different ways and am currently shooting in the dark.
